title: py32-hal's half-duplex UART write turns the receiver off and never turns it back on, so a reader that is already waiting stops receiving.
summary: On 2026-07-15 embassy (commit 082d3b8a) changed UartTx::write and blocking_write so that, in half-duplex mode, they wait for the transmission to finish and then re-enable the receiver (RE) and disable the transmitter (TE). py32-hal, whose USART driver is copied from embassy, still clears RE at the start of every half-duplex write and leaves it to the next read() call to turn it back on; its ring-buffered reader never turns it back on. If the TX and RX halves of a split half-duplex Uart run in separate tasks, a reader that is already waiting never sees data again after the first write, so the receive side stops for good. The fix uses only functions and register fields that py32-hal already has (flush, blocking_flush, CR3.HDSEL, CR1.RE/TE).

fix.subject: stm32/usart: restore RE after a half-duplex write instead of relying on the next read()

evidence: The picked hunk adds `let half_duplex = r.cr3().read().hdsel();` to UartTx::blocking_write; it is the first half of the fix whose message says "UartTx::write/blocking_write now restore RE (and clear TE) for half-duplex links themselves once the transmission genuinely completes", and the same commit adds `if half_duplex { blocking_flush(...)?; set_re(true); set_te(false) }` after the loop (still present in embassy's blocking_write_helper, mod.rs:833-853). py32-hal's UartTx::blocking_write (src/usart/mod.rs:503) and async write (line 394) are the pre-fix logic: in half-duplex (hdsel) they set TE and clear RE, send the bytes and return without restoring RE; RE is only turned back on by the entry checks of UartRx::inner_read_run (line 641) and blocking_read (line 978), and RingBufferedUartRx::read (ringbuffered.rs:148) never re-enables it at all. py32-hal supports the concurrent case the commit describes: Uart::split is documented as useful for two tasks (line 1300) and UartRx::into_ring_buffered exists, so a reader already parked in a read is left with the receiver disabled. Everything the fix needs exists on the py32 side (the hdsel field, flush(info, state) at line 534, blocking_flush(info) at line 563) and nothing there restores RE after a write in another way.

title: py32-hal's DMA interrupt handler uses else-if, so a pending half-transfer flag hides the transfer-complete flag until a second interrupt.
summary: On 2026-03-17 embassy (commit 1b36829e) replaced the else-if chain in the DMA interrupt handler with two separate checks, so that when the half-transfer and transfer-complete flags are both set the handler clears both and counts the finished buffer lap in one pass. py32-hal's AnyChannel::on_irq still has the else-if: with both flags set it clears only the half-transfer flag, and the transfer-complete flag and the lap counter wait for a second interrupt. In between, the ring buffer's position sync sees the DMA position wrap with no lap counted and falls back to cap - 1, so it briefly reports less received data than there is and read_exact waits one extra round. Nothing is lost, so the effect is a short extra delay, and the embassy change can be copied directly.

fix.subject: dma: fix else-if in on_irq allowing HTIF to mask TCIF

evidence: The embassy commit (message "dma: fix else-if in on_irq allowing HTIF to mask TCIF") replaces `} else if isr.tcif(...)` with a separate `if` plus an activity flag, because "When both HTIF and TCIF are set simultaneously ... the previous else-if chain only cleared HTIF and returned without incrementing complete_count"; embassy still has this at dma_bdma/mod.rs:57-77. py32-hal's AnyChannel::on_irq (src/dma/dma.rs:170-188) is the same pre-fix logic: the half-transfer branch at line 170 and the transfer-complete branch, which acknowledges TCIF and increments complete_count (line 178), are joined by `} else if` at line 173. py32-hal's ring buffers enable both interrupts in circular mode (src/dma/dma.rs:585-587), and its dma_sync has the same fallback the commit message describes, `if pos < self.pos && count_diff == 0 { cap - 1 }` (src/dma/ringbuffer/mod.rs:55-56), so the same temporary under-report can happen. The fix only restructures existing branches and uses nothing py32-hal lacks; the extra NDTR check in py32-hal's transfer-complete branch is unaffected.
impact_note: The transfer-complete flag stays pending and is handled by a second interrupt right afterwards, so no data is lost; the ring buffer only briefly reports less data than it holds and read_exact waits one extra wake-up.

title: SimplePwm on a 32-bit timer (TIM2 on PY32F072) can set ARR above 0xFFFF, so max_duty_cycle() and set_duty_cycle() hit the u16 assert and panic.
summary: Embassy fixed this in November 2024 (commit 3402e76) by making SimplePwm and ComplementaryPwm compute the prescaler for a 16-bit period even on 32-bit timers, because a large ARR made max_duty_cycle() panic on its assert!(max < u16::MAX as u32); embassy has since reworked the code again and its max_duty_cycle now returns u32. py32-hal still has the pre-fix code: SimplePwm::set_frequency calls the generic set_frequency, whose 32-bit branch never raises the prescaler, while max_duty_cycle keeps the u16 assert. Since the pinned py32-hal commit switched to metapac data that makes TIM2 on PY32F072 a 32-bit GP32 timer, a SimplePwm on TIM2 at a low enough frequency (timer clock divided by frequency above 65535) panics as soon as the duty cycle is read or set. The port is the SimplePwm/low_level part of the patch with py32's cfg(any(py32f071, py32f072)) in place of cfg(not(stm32l0)); the ComplementaryPwm part does not apply because py32's advanced timers are all 16-bit. The metapac data itself is not in the repository, so the TIM2 classification rests on the commit message and README.

fix.subject: stm32/timer: avoid max_compare_value >= u16::MAX

evidence: The embassy commit fixes a real panic: "With STM32 32 bits timers, the max_compare_value (AKA, ARR register) can currently be set greater than u16::MAX, which leads to the following assert!(max < u16::MAX as u32) in max_duty_cycle()"; it makes PWM set_frequency limit ARR to 16 bits. In py32-hal, SimplePwm::set_frequency (simple_pwm.rs line 286) still calls the generic inner.set_frequency, whose Bits32 branch in Timer::set_frequency (low_level.rs lines 272-279) divides by 1 << 32 so the prescaler stays 0 and ARR can be any u32, and both max_duty_cycle() functions (simple_pwm.rs lines 89 and 294) keep the same assert, with the same TODO "prevent ARR = u16::MAX?" at line 280; this is the same logic as embassy before the fix and nothing else bounds ARR. The 32-bit path is reachable: TimerBits::Bits32 is compiled for py32f071/py32f072 (mod.rs line 53), a TIM_GP32 timer gets BITS = Bits32 and implements GeneralInstance4Channel, so it can drive SimplePwm (mod.rs lines 282-288), and the pinned py32-hal commit merges PR py32f072-tim-gp32 whose only change, "add tim2 gp32 data changes", bumps the metapac to rev d70fd58 (Cargo.toml line 18); the README's TODO list also names "F072 TIM2(GP32) support". Only the SimplePwm part applies: ComplementaryPwm needs AdvancedInstance4Channel, which py32 implements only for 1CH_CMP/2CH_CMP/ADV timers that are all Bits16, so the complementary_pwm.rs hunk is not applicable. Confidence is medium because the metapac data itself is not in the repository; the TIM2 classification is inferred from the commit message and README.

title: c0's I2C nonblocking driver still uses the old field-style register access (and the old I2C peripheral name), so the i2c-nonblocking feature most likely does not compile.
summary: In January 2025 the g0 HAL fixed its I2C nonblocking driver (commit 3598a5d, "fix i2c-nonblocking") by converting all register accesses from the old field style (i2c.cr1.modify) to the accessor methods (i2c.cr1().modify) that its newer PAC uses. The c0 HAL carries a copy of the same driver, and at the pinned commit src/i2c/nonblocking.rs still has the field-style accesses, even though c0's own PAC update converted every other module, including i2c/blocking.rs; it also still imports the peripheral as I2C while the blocking driver uses I2C1. Anyone selecting the non-default i2c-nonblocking feature will most likely get compile errors, and c0's CI does not build that feature. The port is the same mechanical conversion, adapted to c0's file (which also needs the I2C to I2C1 rename); this conclusion comes from reading code only, as nothing was compiled.

The module is compiled only with the i2c-nonblocking feature (mod.rs lines 4-5; Cargo.toml default is i2c-blocking) and c0's CI only runs cargo check with chip features, so the breakage is unseen. Nothing on the c0 side makes the fix inapplicable: it has the same feature and the same driver structure; the failure is a build error, not wrong runtime behaviour, and is inferred from code since nothing is compiled here.
impact_note: It only breaks compilation of the optional i2c-nonblocking feature; the field-to-method change does not alter what is written to the registers.

title: The buffered UART interrupt handler treats any set TC flag as end of transmission even when TCIE was not armed, so flush() can finish before the queued bytes are sent.
summary: Embassy fixed its buffered UART in November 2025 (commit 4e80834) so the interrupt handler only reports transmission complete when the TC flag is set and the TC interrupt was actually enabled by the driver after loading the last byte. py32-hal's buffered UART, copied from the older embassy code, still checks only the TC flag: whenever the shared interrupt runs (receive, idle, TX-empty, or the software pend issued by write()) while TC happens to be set, it marks the transmission as done and wakes flush(). As a result flush() can return while bytes are still in the TX buffer, which matters to callers that switch an RS-485 direction pin, power down or reconfigure the UART after flushing. The port is the one-line condition change; how often a stale TC is present depends on hardware timing that the repository does not show.

fix.subject: fix: fix incorrect logic for buffered usart transmission complete.

evidence: Embassy's fix ("fix incorrect logic for buffered usart transmission complete") changes the TC branch of the buffered UART interrupt handler from if sr_val.tc() to if sr_val.tc() && r.cr1().read().tcie(), so transmission-complete is only reported when the driver itself armed TCIE after loading the last byte (embassy buffered.rs line 105 now). py32-hal's on_interrupt in src/usart/buffered.rs is the same pre-fix code: at line 87 it tests only the TC status bit, then clears TC, disables TCIE, sets tx_done = true and wakes the TX waker (lines 89-95), while TCIE is armed only when the last byte is written (lines 109-111). The handler is shared with RXNE/IDLE/TXE interrupts and is also pended by write() right after write() sets tx_done = false (lines 493 and 509), so any time the TC status bit is already set without TCIE being armed (a stale TC, or TC set between bytes while more data is queued), tx_done becomes true and flush() (line 521) returns before the queued bytes are sent. I checked what could make it inapplicable: py32's CR1 has the TCIE bit (the driver calls set_tcie), clear_interrupt_flags is a no-op on this v1-style USART (usart/mod.rs line 1640) so nothing else clears or filters TC, and no other guard exists. When exactly the TC bit is set is hardware behaviour not visible in the repository, hence medium confidence.

title: stm32c0xx-hal's SPI read takes the address of a temporary register reference, so it does not return the byte received in the SPI data register.
summary: stm32g0xx-hal fixed this on 2024-12-19 (5c38934, 'fix SPI transfer') after its PAC upgrade turned the `dr` field into a `dr()` method: `&self.spi.dr() as *const _ as *const u8` then points at the temporary reference returned by `dr()` instead of at the data register, so the fix reads `self.spi.dr().read().bits() as u8` (g0 later moved to an 8-bit `dr8()` accessor and had to fix a reintroduced copy once more). stm32c0xx-hal went through the same mechanical edit in its 'update PAC version' commit and its FullDuplex read at src/spi.rs line 248 still uses the pre-fix expression. Left as is, every byte returned by read(), and therefore by the blocking SPI transfer built on it, comes from that temporary pointer value rather than from the received SPI data. The c0 PAC source is not in the repository, so it cannot be checked whether it also offers g0's `dr8()` alias; the 5c38934 form only needs `dr()`, which c0 already calls.

fix.subject: fix SPI transfer

evidence: In stm32g0xx-hal, commit 1a2fbea ('Switch to stm32g0-staging') mechanically turned `&self.spi.dr as *const _ as *const u8` into `&self.spi.dr() as *const _ as *const u8`; with `dr()` a method call, `&` takes the address of the temporary register reference it returns, not of the DR register, and three days later 5c38934 ('fix SPI transfer') replaced the byte read with `self.spi.dr().read().bits() as u8` (g0 even fixed a reintroduced copy again in 865ed9d 'fix spi', and its pinned code reads `self.spi.dr8().read().bits() as u8`). stm32c0xx-hal made the identical mechanical change in its 'update PAC version' commit 2d433f6, and its `FullDuplex::read` (src/spi.rs lines 235-248) still has exactly the pre-fix logic: check SR error flags, then on RXNE `ptr::read_volatile(&self.spi.dr() as *const _ as *const u8)`. c0 uses the same method-style register API (`self.spi.sr().read()` at line 236, `self.spi.dr().write(...)` at line 266), so nothing makes the problem absent there, and no other read path exists; the blocking transfer (`transfer::Default<u8>`, line 275) is built on this read. The g0 send-side change from the same commit was not picked and is not judged here.

title: py32-hal's BufferedUartRx embedded-hal serial read() reads the UART data register directly instead of the interrupt-filled receive buffer.
summary: Embassy fixed this on 2025-02-24 (commit 76756ee7): the embedded-hal 0.2 / embedded-hal-nb non-blocking read of BufferedUartRx now takes bytes from the ring buffer that the UART interrupt fills. py32-hal's copy in src/usart/buffered.rs (lines 739-765) still checks the status register and reads the data register itself, while its interrupt handler is reading the same data register into the ring buffer. As a result, code that uses nb::block!(rx.read()) on a py32 buffered UART will mostly get WouldBlock and never see the bytes already received into the buffer, and a direct read can occasionally take a byte away from the interrupt handler, so received data is effectively lost through this API. The fix carries over with only the names unchanged, because py32-hal uses the same State and RingBuffer types as embassy.

fix.subject: fix: BufferedUartRx embedded_hal_nb::serial::Read impl

evidence: The embassy commit (message: "fix: BufferedUartRx embedded_hal_nb::serial::Read impl") replaced the body of BufferedUartRx's embedded_hal_02 serial Read impl, which polled SR and read RDR straight from the hardware, with a read from the interrupt-filled rx ring buffer (pop_one, pending the interrupt when the buffer was full); the embedded_hal_nb Read impl delegates to it. py32-hal's src/usart/buffered.rs still has the pre-fix body unchanged in the same impl (lines 739-765), and its embedded_hal_nb Read impls for BufferedUartRx and BufferedUart (lines 825-829, 843-847) delegate to it. Its interrupt handler is the same as embassy's pre-fix one: RXNE interrupts are enabled in enable_and_configure (line 362) and on_interrupt reads RDR on RXNE and pushes the byte into state.rx_buf (lines 44-45, 63-69), so the direct register read competes with the ISR, normally finds RXNE already cleared and returns WouldBlock while received bytes stay in the ring buffer and are never returned through this API. Nothing hardware-specific is involved: py32-hal depends unconditionally on embedded-hal 0.2 and embedded-hal-nb (Cargo.toml lines 28, 31) and uses the same State/RingBuffer types, and the ring buffer methods the fix uses (pop_one, is_full) exist in embassy-hal-internal 0.5, the version py32-hal uses. Embassy later deleted these trait impls entirely in an API cleanup (130d33053 "stm32: align to api guidelines"), which is why the fixed side no longer has the lines, but py32-hal still exposes the impls with the old body.

title: py32-hal's buffered UART blocking flush returns when the software buffer is empty, before the last bytes have actually been transmitted.
summary: Embassy fixed this on 2025-09-10 (commit 88c42745, PR #4648): the buffered UART's blocking_flush now waits for the transmission-complete flag set by the TC interrupt, and blocking_write clears that flag first. py32-hal copied the async version of this logic, but its blocking_flush (src/usart/buffered.rs line 555) still only waits until the ring buffer is empty, and blocking_write never clears the flag. Without the fix, flush() on the blocking, embedded-io and embedded-hal paths returns while the final byte or two are still being shifted out, so anything done right after flush, such as releasing an RS-485 driver-enable line, changing the baud rate, entering low power or dropping the UART (which turns off its clock), can truncate the end of the message. The upstream patch, both the blocking_flush line and the blocking_write line, applies to py32-hal unchanged; embassy later hardened the same flag logic against races (4e808345, fe45c6e7), which a port may also want to take.

fix.subject: stm32/usart: fix blocking flush

evidence: Embassy's commit (message: "stm32/usart: fix blocking flush. The PR in #2416 fixes buffered usart flushing, but only for the async functions. This commit introduces the same fixes to the blocking functions.") changes BufferedUartTx::blocking_flush to wait for state.tx_done, which the TC interrupt sets, instead of returning as soon as the software tx ring buffer is empty, and also clears tx_done at the start of blocking_write. py32-hal's blocking_flush (src/usart/buffered.rs lines 552-559) is identical to embassy's pre-fix code and returns when state.tx_buf.is_empty(), i.e. once the last byte has merely been handed to the data register, not when it has been shifted out. py32-hal already has everything the fix relies on: the State.tx_done flag (initialised true, line 143), an ISR that arms TCIE when the last byte is sent and sets tx_done on TC (lines 95, 111), and an async flush that already waits on tx_done (line 521), so only the async half of #2416 was carried over; its blocking_write (line 531) does not clear tx_done either. blocking_flush is what embedded_io::Write::flush and the embedded-hal 0.2/nb flush impls call (e.g. line 725), so code that flushes and then releases an RS-485 driver, changes the baud rate or drops the UART (which disables the peripheral clock, line 627) can cut off the final byte(s). Embassy still uses the tx_done-based blocking_flush at the pinned commit (later hardened in 4e808345 and fe45c6e7).

title: py32-hal's timer get_frequency divides by ARR instead of ARR + 1, so it reports a frequency that is too high and divides by zero when ARR is 0.
summary: Embassy fixed stm32/timer get_frequency on 2026-07-13 (commit c184286a) so that it divides by (arr + 1), matching how the period is programmed as ARR + 1 counts. py32-hal's Timer::get_frequency in src/timer/low_level.rs still computes timer_f / arr / (psc + 1) in both its 16-bit and 32-bit arms, while its own set_frequency writes arr = divide_by - 1. As a result the embedded-hal Pwm get_period of SimplePwm and ComplementaryPwm reports a frequency that is too high by a factor (arr + 1) / arr: negligible for large ARR, but twice the real value at ARR = 1, and a division-by-zero panic at ARR = 0. Porting needs a small change: the 16-bit arm reads ARR as u16 and ARR can be u16::MAX, so it should be widened to u32 before adding 1.

fix.subject: stm32/timer: fix get_frequency

evidence: Embassy commit 'stm32/timer: fix get_frequency' changed timer_f / arr / (psc + 1) to timer_f / (arr + 1) / (psc + 1), because ARR holds the period minus one (embassy documents the achieved period as (psc + 1) * (arr + 1)); embassy still has the corrected edge-aligned formula at line 813 of its pinned low_level.rs. py32-hal's Timer::get_frequency in src/timer/low_level.rs still has the identical pre-fix expression in both the 16-bit arm (line 344) and the 32-bit arm (line 352), reading arr and psc the same way, and its own set_frequency uses the same convention: it writes arr = divide_by - 1 with the comment 'the timer counts 0..=arr, we want it to count 0..divide_by'. Nothing on the py32 side compensates: Hertz division is plain integer division (Hertz(self.0 / rhs)), and SimplePwm::get_period and ComplementaryPwm::get_period return get_frequency() directly, so they report a frequency that is too high by a factor (arr + 1) / arr and divide by zero when ARR is 0. The fix needs no register, feature or chip difference that py32 lacks; the only adaptation is that the 16-bit arm reads ARR as u16 and set_frequency can produce ARR = u16::MAX (SimplePwm even has 'TODO: prevent ARR = u16::MAX?'), so arr must be widened to u32 before adding 1.

title: embassy-rp declares the RP2040 boot-ROM function float_to_fix64 as returning f32 instead of i64, so callers get a wrong value.
summary: rp-hal fixed the declaration of the RP2040 boot-ROM function float_to_fix64 on 2024-04-01 (commit caa0ea02), changing its return type from f32 to i64 because the old type was 'at odds with the definition in the SDK'. embassy-rp's copy in src/rom_data/rp2040.rs still declares it as returning f32, although its own doc comment says the result is a clamped signed 64-bit integer and the neighbouring float_to_int64 and double_to_fix64 return i64. The public function embassy_rp::rom_data::float_funcs::float_to_fix64 calls the ROM through that wrong signature, so a caller gets the integer result reinterpreted as a 32-bit float with the upper half lost. Nothing inside embassy-rp calls this function, so only application code that uses it directly is affected; the fix is a one-word change of the return type.

title: py32-hal's complementary PWM dead-time encoder leaves out the DTG mode bits for long dead times, so the timer inserts a much shorter dead time than requested.
summary: embassy-stm32 fixed compute_dead_time_value in April 2025 (commit d1555f4) by setting the DTG[7:5] mode bits (110 and 111) for dead times of 255 ticks and more, and its later rewrite still sets them. py32-hal copied the function from embassy-stm32 in November 2024 and still has the pre-fix lines, with a comment that documents the same DTG encoding. When the chosen encoding falls in the 110 or 111 range (for example a request of 400 ticks, or large requests above about 1020 ticks), the value written to BDTR.DTG is read by the timer as a plain 0xx count, so the real dead time is a fraction of the requested one (82 instead of 400 tDTS). The 10x range is not affected. The PY32 timer register description is in the external py32-metapac crate, so the match of the encoding rests on the copied comment and the identical field name.

fix.subject: Dead-time computation in complementary PWM fixed (missing DTG msbs added)

evidence: The embassy commit 'Dead-time computation in complementary PWM fixed (missing DTG msbs added)' ORs the DTG[7:5] mode bits into the value returned by compute_dead_time_value; for the 110 and 111 ranges the old value 32 + target/8 (or /16) lacks those bits, while the 10x change is a no-op because 64 + target/2 already lies in 128..191. py32-hal copied this function from embassy-stm32 and still has the exact pre-fix lines (src/timer/complementary_pwm.rs lines 251, 253, 255) in the same function, whose own comment documents the same encoding (lines 215-216), and set_dead_time passes the result straight to BDTR.DTG (low_level.rs line 664); the module is built unconditionally. For example a request of 400 ticks returns DTG = 82 (its own test at line 311 expects exactly this), which under the documented encoding is a 0xx value meaning 82 tDTS instead of 400. Nothing in py32-hal handles the mode bits another way; the only gap in evidence is that the PY32 register description lives in the external py32-metapac crate, so the encoding match rests on the copied comment and the identical BDTR.DTG field.

title: py32-hal's non-blocking serial write on UartTx blocks until the transmit register is free instead of returning WouldBlock.
summary: On 2025-07-03 embassy-stm32 fixed its `embedded_hal_nb::serial::Write` impl for `UartTx`: `write` now calls a new `nb_write` that returns WouldBlock when TXE is not set, where before it called `blocking_write`. py32-hal, which copied this USART driver from embassy-stm32, still has the old body, so every non-blocking `write` busy-waits on TXE with no timeout. The byte is still sent correctly, but code that polls the non-blocking API (for example a main loop that does other work while waiting) is stalled for each byte, and for as long as transmission is held up. title: embassy-stm32 BufferedUartTx write() and flush() register the TX waker only after checking the buffer state, so a TX-complete wake that arrives in between is lost and the task can hang.
summary: On 2026-09-25 embassy-rp (commit f1fff55) moved the TX waker registration in its buffered UART write() and flush() ahead of the state check, because an interrupt that drained the ring and woke in between left the writer parked forever. embassy-stm32's buffered USART at the pinned commit still checks first and registers only on the pending path, in write() at line 861 and in flush() at line 881, and its interrupt wakes the TX waker only once, when TC fires with an empty ring. If that wake falls between the check and the registration, write() or flush() can stay pending until some unrelated event re-polls the task, so for example an RS-485 sender waiting in flush() stalls. The race depends on interrupt timing and was judged from code reading only; the fix is to register the waker before the check, as rp now does.

fix.subject: fix(rp): register TX waker before checking buffered-uart state

evidence: The rp commit message says the irq handler "could drain the TX ring and wake between a failed push and the waker registration" and that its final drain does not wake again, parking the writer forever; the fix moves state.tx_waker.register(cx.waker()) in front of the check in write() and says "Same fix for flush()". embassy-stm32's BufferedUartTx::write() still calls tx_writer.push_slice() first and registers the tx_waker only inside if data.is_empty() (line 861), and flush() still loads tx_done first and registers only inside if !tx_done (line 881), which is the same check-then-register order as the rp code before the fix. In the stm32 interrupt handler the only tx_waker.wake() for this State is in the TC branch when tx_buf is empty (line 121), which also clears TCIE, so it is a one-shot final wake just like rp's final drain; if it lands between the check and the register (for example on the first wait, when no waker is stored yet), nothing wakes the task again. Both drivers use the same embassy_sync AtomicWaker, the stm32 code neither re-checks after registering nor polls, and nothing hardware-specific is involved; confidence is medium only because the race depends on interrupt timing and cannot be shown by reading alone.

title: hpm-hal BufferedUartTx clears tx_done and commits new bytes in two separate steps and only kicks TX when the ring looked empty, so flush() can return before queued bytes are sent.
summary: embassy-stm32 fixed this on 2026-10-16 (commit fe45c6e) after a stress test lost the tail of 2-4 replies in every 600 at 1 Mbaud: writes now clear tx_done and commit the bytes in one critical section and always kick the interrupt. hpm-hal's buffered UART, built on the same code, still clears tx_done, samples whether the ring is empty, copies, commits and kicks only if the ring looked empty, while its THRE interrupt marks the transfer done whenever it finds the ring empty. If that interrupt lands inside a write, flush() can return while bytes are still queued, so on RS-485 the driver-enable line can drop early and cut off the end of the frame; in the stale-empty case the new bytes can also sit in the ring with the TX interrupt disabled until some other UART interrupt runs. This was judged from code reading only; the timing window is small and was not reproduced on hpm hardware.

fix.subject: stm32/usart: fix early BufferedUart flush

evidence: The embassy commit message says that when the interrupt drains earlier data before the next write lands, TC "sets tx_done with data still queued, so flush() returns before the last bytes are out"; the picked hunks drop the separate tx_done.store(false) and the empty snapshot in write() and blocking_write(), and replace push_done plus a kick only-if-empty with commit_tx (tx_done clear and push_done in one critical section) followed by an unconditional interrupt pend. hpm-hal's BufferedUartTx::write() and blocking_write() still have the pre-fix shape: tx_done.store(false) at lines 427/479, let empty = state.tx_buf.is_empty() at 429/481, tx_writer.push_done(n) at 440/488 outside any critical section, and a kick only if empty at 442/490. Its interrupt handler sets tx_done = true and disables ETHEI whenever THRE is seen with an empty ring (lines 116-117), so if that runs between the store(false) and push_done the new bytes are queued while tx_done is already true and flush() (line 465) returns at once; if empty was sampled as false and the ring drains before push_done, there is no kick and the bytes stay in the ring with the THRE interrupt off. hpm already reports done only when the ring is empty, so only the write-side part of the fix is needed, adapted to its direct first-byte kick or to self.info.interrupt.pend(), which this file already uses, and critical_section is already a dependency; confidence is medium because the hardware path (THRE instead of TC) differs and the race is judged from code only.

title: py32-hal BufferedUartTx still has the pre-fix write path and TC handler, so tx_done can be set while bytes are still queued and flush() returns early.
summary: embassy-stm32 fixed this on 2026-10-16 (commit fe45c6e): writes now clear tx_done and commit the bytes in one critical section and always pend the interrupt, and the TC handler reports done only when the TX ring is empty. py32-hal's buffered USART is a copy of the older embassy-stm32 code and still has every pre-fix piece: a separate tx_done clear and push, a pend only when the ring looked empty, and a TC handler that sets tx_done unconditionally. The race is timing-dependent (the embassy author saw it in 2-4 of 600 replies at 1 Mbaud), and this verdict comes from code reading only.

evidence: The embassy commit message says that when the interrupt drains the first part of a wrapped write before the second lands, "it arms TCIE and stops, and TC then sets tx_done with data still queued, so flush() returns before the last bytes are out"; the picked hunks remove the separate tx_done.store(false) and the empty snapshot in write() and blocking_write(), and replace push_done plus a pend only-if-empty with commit_tx (tx_done clear and push_done in one critical section) and an unconditional pend. py32-hal's buffered.rs, whose header says it is modified from embassy-stm32, still has exactly the pre-fix write(): tx_done.store(false) at line 493, let empty at 495, tx_writer.push_done(n) at 506 and a pend only if empty at 508-509, and blocking_write() has the same empty snapshot, push_done and conditional pend (534, 541, 543). title: Calling set_config on a half-duplex UART in py32-hal clears the half-duplex bit and silently switches it back to full-duplex.
summary: embassy-stm32 fixed this on 2026-06-02 (commit 013fc0d) by making configure keep half-duplex mode when the HDSEL bit is already set, because users cannot set the private duplex field in a Config they pass to set_config. py32-hal's configure still takes half-duplex mode only from its private half_duplex field, which is false in any Config a user can build, and writes it straight into HDSEL. So changing, for example, the baud rate of a UART created with new_half_duplex or new_blocking_half_duplex clears HDSEL and enables TE/RE as for full-duplex. The read and write paths only switch direction when HDSEL is set, so the single-wire link stops working as half-duplex without any error. The embassy patch can be carried over with only the field name changed.

fix.subject: stm32: Fix half-duplex uart reconfigure

evidence: The embassy commit 'stm32: Fix half-duplex uart reconfigure' explains that the duplex config field 'is private and defaults to Full, so a user-supplied Config passed to set_config/reconfigure cannot express half-duplex', and changes configure to use 'config.duplex.is_half() || r.cr3().read().hdsel()' for both the HDSEL write and the TE/RE choice. py32-hal's configure in src/usart/mod.rs is the same logic before the fix: it writes 'w.set_hdsel(config.half_duplex)' and branches on 'if config.half_duplex', where half_duplex is a private field (commented 'private: set by new_half_duplex, not by the user.') that defaults to false and is only set to true on the by-value copy inside new_half_duplex and new_blocking_half_duplex. Every public set_config (Uart via SetConfig, UartTx, UartRx) calls reconfigure, which calls configure(info, kernel_clock, config, cr.re(), cr.te()) with the user's Config, so HDSEL is cleared and TE/RE are set as for full-duplex. Nothing else in py32-hal preserves HDSEL, and the fix needs only reading CR3.HDSEL, which py32-hal already does in its read and write paths, so there is no hardware or feature reason for it not to apply.

title: The STM32C0 SPI driver likely reads the wrong address when receiving and writes the data register at full width, which stm32g0xx-hal fixed by moving both accesses to the 8-bit dr8() register.
summary: stm32g0xx-hal moved its SPI byte read and write onto the 8-bit dr8() data register on 2024-12-19 (this commit, following 'fix SPI transfer' the same day), and did so again in 865ed9d after a merge had brought the old lines back. stm32c0xx-hal still has the code from before both fixes: read() does ptr::read_volatile(&self.spi.dr() as *const _ as *const u8), which reads the temporary reference returned by dr() instead of the register, and send() writes the data register at full width. If this is not fixed, read(), and the blocking transfer and write that call it, most likely return a constant byte instead of the received data, and send() keeps the full-width write that G0 replaced with a byte-wide one. The change has to be adapted to C0's embedded-hal 0.2 read/send, and the repository does not show whether the stm32c0 0.16 PAC provides dr8(); if it does not, a byte pointer taken from the register address is needed.

fix.subject: fix CRC

evidence: G0's spi.rs hunks switch receive_byte from a full-width dr().read() to dr8().read() and send_byte to dr8().write(), so both SPI data-register accesses become 8-bit. Both HALs program the same SPI fields for 8-bit frames (cr2 frxth set, ds 0b111), and C0's own comment says only one byte should be read, so nothing in the repository suggests C0 does not need byte-wide accesses. Whether the stm32c0 0.16 PAC offers dr8() is not visible in the repository, so the port has to be adapted.

title: The imxrt LPI2C interrupt handler does not end a transfer on a NACK or lost arbitration, so later interrupts can keep sending the remaining bytes and messages.
summary: In September 2024 the imx9 LPI2C driver (commit 08949dec, 'Cleanups and error fixes') rewrote its interrupt handler so that on an error it flushes the TX/RX FIFOs, clears all error flags, zeroes the remaining message and byte counts and ends the transfer, sending STOP if none was seen. The imxrt LPI2C driver still has the old handler: on NACK or lost arbitration it records the status, queues STOP only if the message lacks I2C_M_NOSTOP and clears the flags, but leaves the counts, FIFOs and TX/RX interrupts as they are and wakes the caller only when end-of-packet and STOP are seen together. As a result, after an error later interrupts can keep queuing the remaining bytes and start the next messages on the bus, and with I2C_M_NOSTOP no STOP is sent, so the caller may only get a timeout instead of a quick error. The exact bus effect depends on controller behaviour the repository does not document, and the imx9 rewrite also changed how messages are chained and was refined by later commits (one uses an ABORT bit imxrt does not define), so only the error-path part should be carried over, with testing on hardware.

title: The AT32 window watchdog reports a wrong time left in WDIOC_GETSTATUS instead of the time remaining before reset.
summary: On 2026-10-20 commit 14f2daaa2 fixed stm32_getstatus() in the shared STM32 WWDG driver, which reported the time elapsed since the last keepalive as timeleft: it now takes the counter value above WWDG_CR_T_MAX, scales it by the timeout, and prints timeleft instead of the flags. The AT32 WWDG driver, a copy of the same driver with the same register definitions, still has the old variables and formula, and its elapsed value 'priv->reload - reload' even lacks the T_RESET bit, so the subtraction goes negative and wraps. As a result WDIOC_GETSTATUS and reads of the watchdog device return a meaningless time left on AT32, and the debug print shows the flags in place of the time left; the reset timing itself is not affected. The new lines carry over with only the stm32 names changed to at32. The AT32 independent watchdog (at32_iwdg.c), also in this packet, already computes the time left from system ticks and needs no change.

fix.subject: arch/arm/src/common/stm32: fix WWDG time left in WDIOC_GETSTATUS

evidence: The picked hunk is the declaration half of the stm32_getstatus fix (elapsed/reload become remaining/counter for the new computation in the same function); the commit message says 'stm32_getstatus() returned the time elapsed since the last keepalive as timeleft' and that 'the time left is the ticks above T_MAX scaled by the timeout', and also 'The debug print also showed the flags instead of the time left.' at32_wwdg.c is the same WWDG driver: at32_start/at32_keepalive load WWDG_CR_T_RESET | priv->reload, settimeout caps priv->reload at WWDG_CR_T_MAX, at32_wdg.h defines the same T_MASK/T_SHIFT/T_MAX (0x3f)/T_RESET (0x40), and at32_getstatus still declares 'uint32_t elapsed; uint16_t reload;' and returns timeout * elapsed / (reload + 1) under the comment 'Get the time remaining'. Its elapsed is computed as 'priv->reload - reload' without the T_RESET bit, so while the counter is at or above 0x40 the subtraction is negative and wraps in uint32_t, which makes the reported timeleft meaningless rather than merely inverted; the debug line still prints status->flags as timeleft. The other file in this packet, at32_iwdg.c, does not need the change: its at32_getstatus measures clock_systime_ticks() since the last ping and already returns priv->timeout - elapsed. Every macro the fix uses exists in arch/arm/src/at32/hardware/at32_wdg.h, so nothing on AT32 makes the fix inapplicable.

title: The GD32W51x window watchdog reports the elapsed time instead of the time left in WDIOC_GETSTATUS.
summary: On 2026-10-20 commit 14f2daaa2 fixed stm32_getstatus() in the STM32 WWDG driver, which returned the time elapsed since the last keepalive as timeleft, by taking the counter value above WWDG_CR_T_MAX instead. The GD32W51x WWDGT driver, added on 2026-10-23 with the same counter scheme (loaded with CNT_RESET | reload, timeout of reload + 1 ticks), still computes 'elapsed = priv->reload - (counter & WWDGT_CTL_CNT_MAX)' and returns timeout * elapsed / (reload + 1) as timeleft. WDIOC_GETSTATUS and reads of the watchdog device therefore report about 0 ms right after a keepalive and nearly the full timeout just before the reset, the reverse of the real time left; the reset timing itself is not affected. The fix carries over by replacing the two computation lines with 'counter > WWDGT_CTL_CNT_MAX ? counter - WWDGT_CTL_CNT_MAX : 0' scaled the same way; the debug-print part of the STM32 fix is not needed because this driver already prints timeleft.

title: The ESP32-C2 Wi-Fi adapter allocates a new interrupt handle on every Wi-Fi start and leaks it because the IRQ already has one registered.
summary: On 2026-09-30 commit 1c6ed642b changed set_intr_wrapper in the esp32, esp32s2, esp32s3, esp32c3 and esp32c6 Wi-Fi adapters to reuse the interrupt handle already registered for the IRQ instead of allocating a new one each time. The ESP32-C2 adapter, added two weeks later, still has the old code: each call allocates a new handle from the kernel heap and passes it to esp_set_handle, which refuses it with -EINVAL because the handle from the first start is still registered, and the new block is never freed. An application that stops and restarts Wi-Fi on ESP32-C2 (for example to save power) therefore loses a few bytes of kernel heap per cycle without bound. The same patch applies with no changes; the only part not visible in the repository is the closed Wi-Fi library itself, whose repeated calls on every start are stated by the fix commit message.

fix.subject: espressif: stop leaking a Wi-Fi interrupt handle on every esp_wifi_start()

evidence: The fix commit says set_intr_wrapper() 'allocates a new intr_handle_data_t from the kernel heap each time the Wi-Fi driver calls it, and the driver calls it on every esp_wifi_start()', while 'clear_intr_wrapper() is a no-op', so 'esp_set_handle() refuses to replace it with -EINVAL, the return value is ignored, and the new block is lost'; the listed hunks look up the vector descriptor first and reuse the handle already registered for the IRQ. The esp32c2 set_intr_wrapper is the pre-fix esp32c3 code line for line: it kmm_calloc()s a new handle on every call, stores get_desc_for_int() into it, and calls esp_set_handle(cpu_no, irq, handle) without checking the result, and its clear_intr_wrapper body is empty. esp32c2 builds the same common esp_irq.c (its Make.defs includes common/espressif/Make.defs, which adds esp_irq.c), whose esp_set_handle returns -EINVAL when the IRQ already has a handle, and no esp32c2 or common Wi-Fi code calls esp_teardown_irq for the Wi-Fi interrupt, while the shared esp_wifi_api_start/esp_wifi_api_stop call esp_wifi_start()/esp_wifi_stop() on each start and stop. Everything the fix uses (esp_get_handle, IRQ_UNMAPPED, get_desc_for_int, kmm_calloc) is available to the esp32c2 adapter, which includes esp_irq.h and already calls get_desc_for_int. The esp32c2 adapter was added on 2026-10-15 by 633d67f88 'arch/risc-v/esp32c2: add wireless adapters', two weeks after the 2026-09-30 fix, which is why the commit message names only esp32, esp32s2, esp32s3, esp32c3 and esp32c6.

title: The ESP32-S2 SPI polling exchange writes up to 3 bytes past the end of the receive buffer when the transfer length is not a multiple of 4.
summary: On 2026-10-23 commit 236b47dd0 changed the ESP32-S3 SPI polling exchange to copy only the bytes left in the last partial 32-bit word, after it was found corrupting the field after the receive buffer on a real board. The ESP32-S2 polling exchange is the same code: its receive loop still copies a full 4-byte word on every step, and its transmit loop still reads a full word from the transmit buffer. Any polled SPI transfer whose byte count is not a multiple of 4 (for example a 61-byte or 3-byte read, which goes through this path when DMA is off or the transfer is under the DMA threshold) therefore writes up to 3 bytes past the caller's receive buffer and reads up to 3 bytes past its transmit buffer, silently corrupting nearby memory. The same two-line change per loop applies with only the names changed.

evidence: The fix commit says esp32s3_spi_poll_exchange() always copies a full 32-bit word, so 'When the transfer length is not a multiple of 4, the last copy reads up to 3 bytes past the end of txbuffer and writes up to 3 bytes past the end of rxbuffer, silently corrupting whatever follows the receive buffer in memory'; the picked hunk limits the final receive copy to chunk = MIN(sizeof(uint32_t), transfer_size - i). The esp32s2 esp32s2_spi_poll_exchange has the same structure: it computes total_bytes = nwords * (priv->nbits / 8), splits it into chunks of transfer_size = MIN(SPI_MAX_BUF_SIZE, bytes_remaining) with SPI_MAX_BUF_SIZE 64 (16 registers W0-W15), and its receive loop runs i in steps of sizeof(uintptr_t) up to transfer_size and does memcpy(rp, &r_wd, sizeof(uintptr_t)) for every step, so a final chunk whose length is not a multiple of 4 writes up to 3 bytes past the end of rxbuffer. Its transmit loop has the matching over-read (memcpy(&w_wd, tp, sizeof(uint32_t)) for every step), which the esp32s3 commit fixed in its other hunk. The function is reached from esp32s2_spi_exchange whenever SPI DMA is off, and with DMA on for every transfer at or below CONFIG_ESP32S2_SPI_DMATHRESHOLD (default 64), and nothing on the esp32s2 side pads or rounds the caller's buffers. The fix needs only MIN and the existing loop variables, both already used in this function, and esp32s2_spi.c has not been touched since the 2026-10-23 esp32s3 fix except for the exchange return type change.

title: The i.MX RT uSDHC driver does not compile with DMA on and the D-cache option off, because it uses priv->rxbuffer outside the CONFIG_ARMV7M_DCACHE guard that declares it.
summary: In August 2024 commit 23e0bf595 fixed a build error in the i.MX9 uSDHC driver: rxbuffer only exists when the data cache is in use, but the DMA preflight check and the receive setup still referred to it. The i.MX RT driver has the same code: rxbuffer is declared only under CONFIG_ARMV7M_DCACHE, yet imxrt_dmapreflight compares the buffer with priv->rxbuffer and imxrt_dmarecvsetup uses sizeof(priv->rxbuffer) in a DEBUGASSERT that is compiled even with assertions off. A configuration with USDHC DMA (default on) and 'Use D-Cache' off (default off) therefore stops with a compile error; the shipped board configurations all enable the D-cache, so only custom configurations hit it. Carrying the fix over means using the imxrt guard CONFIG_ARMV7M_DCACHE instead of CONFIG_ARM64_DCACHE_DISABLE, or declaring rxbuffer for every DMA build.

title: The pic32mx Ethernet driver asserts, or points the RX DMA at address 0, when no free buffer is left to replace a received one.
summary: In October 2026 the pic32mz Ethernet driver (commit 2851f1c09) stopped asserting when no free buffer is left to replace the one in a completed RX descriptor; it now drops the packet and gives the descriptor back with its current buffer, and the current pic32mz code still does this. pic32mx_rxdone still allocates the replacement with pic32mx_allocbuffer, checks it only with DEBUGASSERT, and writes PHYS_ADDR(rxbuffer) into the descriptor. If the free list is empty, a debug build stops on the assertion, and a release build hands the Ethernet DMA a descriptor that points at address 0, so the next frame is written outside the driver's buffers and that address is later treated as a driver buffer. The free list can run short on pic32mx the same way the later pic32mz commit 58b2989c6 describes, because pic32mx_bufferinit re-appends every buffer on each ifup without emptying the list. Confidence is medium because with an intact free list the pool (one buffer per descriptor plus one) should leave exactly one buffer for this allocation, so the failure depends on that buffer loss or a similar leak.

fix.subject: arch/mips/pic32mz: fix the Ethernet driver TX ring, RX buffers and MAC.

evidence: The picked hunk is a behavioural fix: the commit message says 'Drop a received packet instead of asserting when no buffer is free to replace the one in the RX descriptor.' pic32mx_rxdone has the same pre-fix logic: it moves the RX buffer to d_buf, takes a replacement with pic32mx_allocbuffer (sq_remfirst on the free list, documented as returning NULL on failure), only checks it with DEBUGASSERT (which compiles to nothing without CONFIG_DEBUG_ASSERTIONS), and then writes PHYS_ADDR(rxbuffer), i.e. address 0, into the descriptor. The buffer pool (NRXDESC + NTXDESC + 1) and pic32mx_bufferinit are the same as in the pre-fix pic32mz, and bufferinit appends every buffer again on each ifup (also called from the TX-timeout work) without emptying the list, which the later pic32mz commit 58b2989c6 says 'truncates the list and loses buffers', so an empty free list is reachable on pic32mx too. Everything the fix uses exists on pic32mx: pic32mx_rxreturn(rxdesc) has the same one-argument form as the pre-fix pic32mz_rxreturn, NETDEV_RXDROPPED is already used in this function, and the driver has no other handling of a failed allocation at this point.

title: The AT32 WWDG interrupt passes no instance to the watchdog capture callback, so when the IWDG is also registered the auto-monitor stops reloading the WWDG.
summary: In July 2026 commit 2bf7d987 made the common watchdog upper half look up the capture auto-monitor instance from the callback argument, and changed the STM32 WWDG lower halves to pass their own instance (priv) instead of the NULL interrupt argument. at32_wwdg.c still passes arg, which is NULL because its interrupt is attached with a NULL argument. The upper half accepts a NULL argument only when exactly one watchdog is in its capture list, and every registered watchdog is added to that list, so an AT32 build that registers both the IWDG and the WWDG with CONFIG_WATCHDOG_AUTOMONITOR_BY_CAPTURE ignores the WWDG early-wakeup callback and the WWDG resets the board. title: The GD32VW55x WWDGT early-wakeup interrupt passes a NULL context to the watchdog capture callback, so the watchdog core cannot tell which watchdog fired when more than one is registered.
summary: In July 2026 NuttX changed the STM32 WWDG interrupt handlers to pass their own driver instance to the watchdog core's capture callback; the core now looks the watchdog up from that pointer and accepts a NULL pointer only when a single watchdog is in its capture list. title: The AT32 window watchdog is started without clearing a possibly stale early-wakeup flag (EWIF), so the early-warning handler can fire at the wrong time.
summary: In September 2025 (commit 2e85eae6b2ec) the STM32H7 window watchdog driver started clearing the EWIF flag in stm32_start before enabling the watchdog, because the flag can already be set before the watchdog is started; the unified STM32 driver now does the same for every STM32 window watchdog version. The AT32 copy, at32_start in arch/arm/src/at32/at32_wwdg.c, still enables the watchdog straight away without clearing EWIF, while at32_capture enables the early-wakeup interrupt and at32_interrupt calls the user handler whenever EWIF is set. If the flag is stale, the handler can run right away instead of shortly before expiry, and the handler is expected to reload the counter, which causes a reset if a window is configured and the counter is still above it (lines 245-248). Only the one-line flag clear needs porting (modifyreg32(AT32_WWDG_SR, WWDG_SR_EWIF, 0)); the prescaler-range hunks must not be copied because AT32 only has a 2-bit timer base field. The repository does not show whether AT32 hardware can set EWIF before activation, no in-tree board calls at32_wwdginitialize, and outside this candidate at32_getstatus (line 458) still has the pre-fix elapsed formula that the same commit corrected.

title: The AT32 CAN register-debug write helper logs an undeclared variable val, so the driver does not compile with CONFIG_AT32_CAN_REGDEBUG.
summary: In April 2026 commit 369755d fixed stm32can_vputreg in the STM32 CAN driver so that its debug line logs the parameter value instead of the undeclared name val. The AT32 CAN driver is a copy of that code and still has caninfo(..., addr, val) in at32can_vputreg at line 368, whose parameter is named value. With CONFIG_AT32_CAN_REGDEBUG (which requires CONFIG_DEBUG_CAN_INFO) this function is compiled and caninfo becomes a syslog call, so the build stops with an undeclared identifier. Replacing val with value on that line fixes it; builds without the register-debug option are not affected.

With CONFIG_STM32_CAN_REGDEBUG (offered for F7 through the common STM32 Kconfig, and requiring CONFIG_DEBUG_CAN_INFO) the function is compiled and caninfo becomes a syslog call, so the build stops with an undeclared identifier. fix.subject: drivers/can: Fix close drain, write-only reader lifecycle, and STM32 RX header

evidence: The picked hunk changes the log line in stm32can_vputreg(uint32_t addr, uint32_t value) from 'addr, val' to 'addr, value'; the commit message says 'Fix stm32can_vputreg debug log to print the written value (correct parameter name)'. Before the fix val was not declared in that function (it is only a local of stm32can_vgetreg), so the file could not be compiled once the register-debug code is enabled, because caninfo is then a real syslog call (debug.h: '#  define caninfo _info'). The STM32F7 stm32_can.c has the identical function stm32can_vputreg(uint32_t addr, uint32_t value) and line 369 still passes val; line 320 is in stm32can_vgetreg, where val is the declared local holding the register read and is correct. The function is compiled under CONFIG_STM32_CAN_REGDEBUG, which is selectable for F7: ARCH_CHIP_STM32F7 selects ARCH_CHIP_STM32, which sources common/stm32/Kconfig and its Kconfig.can with 'config STM32_CAN_REGDEBUG' (depends on DEBUG_CAN_INFO). An F7 build with that option therefore fails with an undeclared identifier, exactly as the STM32 build did; the one-word fix applies unchanged.

title: The STM32H7 ADC1/ADC2 shared interrupt handler acts on status flags that are not enabled in IER, so it can read data and report samples for an ADC whose interrupt is disabled.
summary: In November 2026 commit 39572c4 changed the STM32H5 adc12_interrupt to mask each ADC's ISR with its IER and to pass only those bits to adc_interrupt, so the shared handler no longer services flags of an ADC that did not raise the interrupt. The STM32H7 adc12_interrupt still computes ISR & ADC_INT_MASK and passes the raw ISR, although on H7 ADC1 and ADC2 share the single vector STM32_IRQ_ADC12. When one ADC is in watchdog mode (EOC removed from IER while it converts continuously) or has its interrupts disabled, any interrupt on the shared vector, or its own watchdog interrupt, still runs the end-of-conversion path for it: the handler reads its data register and pushes samples to its upper half that the driver had switched off. Adding the IER mask to both pending computations and passing pending instead of regval, as in the H5 driver, fixes it.

fix.subject: arch/arm/stm32h5: Fix ADC interrupt dispatch

evidence: The picked hunk changes the ADC1/ADC2 dispatcher adc12_interrupt so that each ADC is serviced only for flags that are set in its ISR and enabled in its IER, and passes that masked value to adc_interrupt instead of the raw ISR; the commit message says 'Only handle ADC interrupts that are enabled in IER, so a shared interrupt no longer services flags of an ADC that did not raise it'. The STM32H7 adc12_interrupt is the same pre-fix code (pending = regval & ADC_INT_MASK at lines 2174/2183, adc_interrupt(&g_adcdevN, regval) at 2177/2186), and on H7 ADC1 and ADC2 really share one vector (both have .irq = STM32_IRQ_ADC12). Flags are set there without being enabled: the ANIOC_WDOG_UPPER/LOWER ioctls call adc_wdog_enable, which turns on continuous conversion and removes ADC_INT_EOC from IER, and adc_rxint(false) clears all IER bits, while the H7 adc_interrupt, like the H5 one, acts on every bit it is given (its EOC branch reads DR and calls au_receive). So an interrupt from the other ADC, or the ADC's own AWD1 interrupt in watchdog mode, still runs the EOC path for an ADC whose EOC interrupt is disabled. The registers the fix reads exist on H7 (STM32_ADC1_IER and STM32_ADC2_IER in hardware/stm32_adc.h), so the change applies as written; the unshared adc3_interrupt (line 2213) has the same pattern but was not part of the H5 change.

title: The STM32L4 ADC1/ADC2 shared interrupt handler acts on status flags that are not enabled in IER, so it can consume conversions and clear flags of an ADC that did not raise the interrupt.
summary: In November 2026 commit 39572c4 changed the STM32H5 adc12_interrupt to mask each ADC's ISR with its IER and to pass only those bits to adc_interrupt. The STM32L4 adc12_interrupt is still the pre-fix code: it treats any set flag in ISR & ADC_INT_MASK as pending, passes the raw ISR to adc_interrupt and then writes it back to clear every flag, while ADC1 and ADC2 share STM32_IRQ_ADC12. When one ADC is in watchdog mode (EOC removed from IER while it converts continuously) or has its interrupts disabled, an interrupt from the other ADC or its own watchdog interrupt still makes the handler read its data register and hand a sample to its upper half, log overruns for an interrupt that was never enabled, and clear its flags. Adding the IER mask to both pending computations and passing pending instead of regval, as in the H5 driver, fixes it; the L4 write-back of the flags can stay inside the same if block.

fix.subject: arch/arm/stm32h5: Fix ADC interrupt dispatch

evidence: The picked hunk changes the ADC1/ADC2 dispatcher adc12_interrupt to service only flags that are set in ISR and enabled in IER, and to pass that masked value to adc_interrupt instead of the raw ISR; the commit message says 'Only handle ADC interrupts that are enabled in IER, so a shared interrupt no longer services flags of an ADC that did not raise it'. The STM32L4 adc12_interrupt has the same pre-fix lines (pending = regval & ADC_INT_MASK at 2236/2249, adc_interrupt(&g_adcdevN, regval) at 2239/2252), additionally writes the raw ISR back to clear it, and on L4 ADC1 and ADC2 share one vector (both have .irq = STM32_IRQ_ADC12). Flags are set there without being enabled: adc_wdog_enable (reached from the ANIOC_WDOG_UPPER/LOWER ioctls) turns on continuous conversion and removes ADC_INT_EOC from IER, adc_rxint(true) enables only EOC (when regular channels exist) and JEOS but never OVR, and adc_rxint(false) clears IER, while the L4 adc_interrupt acts on every bit passed in (its EOC branch reads DR and calls au_receive, its OVR branch logs a warning). So an interrupt from one ADC, or a watchdog interrupt, makes the handler consume a conversion, report an overrun and clear the flags of an ADC whose corresponding interrupt is disabled. STM32_ADC1_IER and STM32_ADC2_IER are defined in hardware/stm32l4_adc.h, so the change carries over as written; the unshared adc3_interrupt (line 2283) has the same pattern but was not part of the H5 change.

title: The stm32l4 USB device driver reads uninitialized setup-request fields when the EP0 handler is re-entered after an OUT data phase.
summary: On 2026-08-21 the common STM32 M0 USB device driver was changed to decode value, index and len from the saved SETUP request after the optional OUT data phase, so these fields are set when stm32_ep0setup is entered a second time to finish an OUT control transfer; the same change fixed Clang builds that treat maybe-uninitialized diagnostics as errors. The stm32l4 driver still decodes them only on the first entry, while stm32_ep0_rdrequest re-enters stm32_ep0setup after the data phase, so the standard-request checks and the response length clamp then read uninitialized stack values. With a compliant host this most likely changes nothing at run time, because SET_DESCRIPTOR, the only standard OUT request with data, is handed to the class driver without using them; a request with an unexpected data phase may be accepted or stalled at random, and the file would hit the same Clang error. The fix can be copied over unchanged.

fix.subject: arm/stm32: Decode saved M0 USB setup requests.

evidence: The l4 stm32_ep0setup is the same code as the pre-fix common M0 driver: value, index and len are declared without an initializer (lines 1703-1705) and are assigned only inside 'if (priv->ep0state != EP0STATE_SETUP_READY)' (lines 1734, 1747-1749). After an OUT data phase, stm32_ep0_rdrequest sets EP0STATE_SETUP_READY (line 1450) and calls stm32_ep0setup again (line 1454), so on that entry the branch is skipped and the standard-request switch reads the uninitialized locals, for example in the SET_ADDRESS check (line 2001), the endpoint-halt checks (lines 1925, 1974), the SET_CONFIGURATION check (line 2081) and the length clamp (line 2167); this is exactly the case the commit message names ('ensures the fields are initialized when the EP0 handler is entered again to complete an OUT control transfer', which 'also fixes Clang builds that treat the resulting maybe-uninitialized diagnostics as errors'). Unlike stm32h5, l4 does not zero these locals at function entry, and the fix uses only GETUINT16, priv->ctrl and STM32_TRACEINTID_EP0SETUPOUT, which l4 already uses, so nothing hardware-specific blocks it. The listed line 2211 is a separate, already correct decode of priv->ctrl.value for SET_ADDRESS in stm32_ep0in and is not part of the problem.
impact_note: With a compliant host the only standard OUT request that has a data phase is SET_DESCRIPTOR, which l4 passes to the class driver without reading these locals, so the garbage values only affect how requests with an unexpected data phase are checked, plus a Clang warnings-as-errors build.

title: The pic32mx Ethernet driver takes received frames out of ring order and loses responses that are waiting for a free TX descriptor.
summary: On 2026-10-10 the pic32mz Ethernet driver fixed its RX path: it now takes RX descriptors in ring order using a ring index, stops receiving while a response waits for a free TX descriptor (and txavail no longer polls over that response), and also processes RX descriptors on overflow and buffer-not-available events. The pic32mx driver, which has the same structure, still scans its RX descriptor ring from index 0 in pic32mx_rxdesc, keeps receiving after pic32mx_response has marked a response as pending and then frees that response's buffer, and reacts only to RXDONE. Under load this can deliver frames out of order and lose responses, and with assertions enabled pic32mx_transmit asserts when txdone sends the pending packet with a NULL buffer. The patch has to be adapted rather than copied: pic32mx never decrements BUFCNT in its RX path, so the BUFCDEC reordering does not carry over and the effect of the overflow-event hunk on pic32mx is not shown by the code, and nothing here was tested on PIC32MX hardware.

title: The RP2040 PWM driver still computes the clock divider and duty-cycle compare values wrongly, and its single-channel build still uses a removed field, the same three bugs fixed in the RP23XX copy.
summary: On 2026-05-25 commit 53ef7c06 fixed three bugs in the RP23XX PWM driver: the period/divider math, the duty-cycle compare formula, and pwm_start still reading info[0].duty after struct pwm_info_s lost its duty member. The RP2040 driver is the same code on the same register layout and still has all three pre-fix versions; it has not been touched since 2026-04-07. With the Pico's 125 MHz clock, almost any requested frequency above about 1.9 kHz gets a divider whose integer part is 0, from about 3.8 kHz the compare value is too large by 65535/TOP so duty cycles come out wrong (larger duties exceed TOP or spill into the channel-B field), and below about 7.5 Hz the divider overflows its 12-bit field. With the default single-channel setting (CONFIG_PWM_NCHANNELS=1) the file does not compile at all. The fix can be copied with only the rp23xx/RP23XX names changed; what the hardware does with an integer divider of 0 is not visible in the repository, but the RP23XX fix treats 0x10 to 0xFFF as the valid range.

title: The i.MX9 FlexCAN TX-deadline timeout handler still aborts the mailbox next to the one that timed out and treats unexpired or already-sent frames as expired, the bugs just fixed in the i.MX RT copy.
summary: On 2026-08-27 commit 58181135 fixed the i.MX RT FlexCAN TX-deadline timeout handling (active when CONFIG_NET_CAN_RAW_TX_DEADLINE is set): the timeout work now aborts mailbox RXMBCOUNT + 1 + mbi, the one whose deadline it checked, compares seconds before microseconds, walks only the real TX ring, and txdone clears the deadline of a finished mailbox. imx9_flexcan.c is a copy of the same driver and still has all of the pre-fix code: deadlines are stored for mailbox RXMBCOUNT + 1 + k but the abort goes to RXMBCOUNT + k, the expiry test fires whenever the current microseconds exceed the deadline's, and finished mailboxes keep their old deadline. When any TX watchdog fires, frames whose deadline has not passed can be aborted, finished mailboxes look expired forever, the abort lands on a neighbouring TX mailbox (possibly one still sending) or on the mailbox reserved for the ER005829 workaround, and the last TX mailbox is never aborted; the commit message reports that on i.MX RT this drove the node error passive and stopped transmission. The imx9 transmit path picks the first free mailbox rather than one above all pending ones, so the permanent allocator lock-up described for i.MX RT may play out differently, but the wrong aborts apply unchanged; the whole commit (including the TXMBRINGSIZE define and the txdone deadline reset) can be copied with only the imxrt/IMXRT names changed.

title: The at32 PWM stop routine leaves the CCR1-CCR4 compare registers set, which stm32f7 started clearing because a channel kept outputting after a STOP in multichannel mode.
summary: In February 2024 (commit 5975b259) stm32f7's pwm_stop gained four writes of 0 to CCR1-CCR4 after the counter and outputs are disabled, because 'when executing pwm STOP command in multichannel mode, the channel still outputting'; stm32h7 and stm32h5 carry the same block at the pinned commit. The at32 pwm_stop (lines 3698-3733) is still the pre-fix copy: it disables the timer interrupts, the counter and the CCER output-enable bits but leaves the compare registers as they were, and nothing else in its stop path clears them. If AT32 timers behave like the STM32 ones here, a PWM STOP in multichannel mode can leave a channel outputting. The port is the same four pwm_putreg calls with AT32_GTIM_CCRn_OFFSET; the repository does not show the hardware cause of the symptom, so whether AT32 parts show it is not confirmed.

fix.subject: arch/stm32f7: Clear all PWM channel when during STOP

evidence: The picked hunk adds writes of 0 to CCR1-CCR4 at the end of the stm32f7 pwm_stop, after the counter and the outputs are disabled; the commit message says 'when executing pwm STOP command in multichannel mode, the channel still outputting. This commit fixes this issue.', and the same block is present in the pwm_stop of stm32h7 and stm32h5 at the pinned commit. The at32 pwm_stop (lines 3698-3733) is the pre-fix copy: it zeroes DIER and SR, calls pwm_timer_enable(dev, false), takes the outputs from pwm_outputs_from_channels and calls pwm_outputs_enable(dev, outputs, false), then leaves the critical section without touching the compare registers; its helpers pwm_timer_enable, pwm_outputs_from_channels and pwm_outputs_enable have the same bodies as on stm32f7 (the other matched lines, 3021/3025 and 3260, are only the same text inside pwm_configure and pwm_timer). Nothing else in the at32 stop path clears CCR1-CCR4 (the driver has no timer reset), and the registers the fix writes exist as AT32_GTIM_CCR1_OFFSET to AT32_GTIM_CCR4_OFFSET in at32/hardware/at32_tim.h. The repository does not explain the hardware cause of the symptom, so it cannot confirm that AT32 timers show exactly the same behaviour; hence medium confidence.

title: The RA4 serial error interrupt handler never clears its ICU IELSR.IR flag, the bug the RA8M1 copy fixed because it livelocked the system on receive errors.
summary: On 2026-10-06 commit 5c3c2cbf fixed the RA8M1 serial driver's up_erinterrupt() to call ra_clear_ir(irq), after hardware testing showed that leaving the ICU IELSR.IR flag set made the NVIC re-enter the handler and livelocked the board on any receive error. The RA4 driver, whose ra_serial.c has the same handler structure, still has the old handler at the pinned commit: up_erinterrupt() only saves and clears the SSR error bits, while its RX and TX handlers already call ra_clear_ir(irq). Because RA4 routes SCIn_ERI through the same IELSR mechanism and has the same ra_clear_ir() helper, a parity, framing or overrun error on an RA4 UART would most likely leave the error interrupt pending and hang the system. Adding ra_clear_ir(irq) at the top of the handler carries over directly; the RA8M1 receive-drain part relies on SCI_B behaviour that the repository does not document for the RA4M1 SCI, so whether it is also needed is uncertain. None of this has been confirmed on RA4 hardware.

title: The legacy ESP32-C3 BLE adapter keeps the saved interrupt state of BLE critical sections in one global variable, so a nested call loses the outer state.
summary: On 2023-11-10 the ESP32 BLE adapter (commit 606190d9b) stopped saving the interrupt state of the controller's interrupt_disable/interrupt_restore callbacks in a single global, because a nested call overwrote the outer saved state; the ESP32, ESP32-S3 and newer ESP32-C3 adapters all still guard against nesting today, now with a nesting counter. The legacy ESP32-C3 adapter still writes every enter_critical_section() result into the one static g_inter_flags and restores that value on every interrupt_restore. If the controller library nests these calls, the outermost interrupt_restore restores the already-disabled state, so interrupts can stay disabled after the BLE critical section ends. The repository cannot show whether the binary legacy ESP32-C3 controller library actually nests these calls; the case rests on the identical callback code and interface and on the fixes made to the sibling adapters.

fix.subject: esp32/ble: fix saving/restoring the interrupt status flags

evidence: The ESP32 commit replaces the single saved flag used by the BLE controller callbacks interrupt_disable()/interrupt_restore() with a list of saved flags because 'calling nested enter_critical_section would overwrite this global variable that was storing the previous flag and, when leaving the last critical section, the restored status would be different from the one expected'. esp32c3-legacy/esp32c3_ble_adapter.c still has exactly the pre-fix code: one static irqstate_t g_inter_flags, interrupt_disable() doing g_inter_flags = enter_critical_section(), interrupt_restore() doing leave_critical_section(g_inter_flags), and both are handed to the BLE controller library through the same ._interrupt_disable/._interrupt_restore callback slots as on ESP32. The fix uses only generic NuttX code (sq_queue lists, or the nesting counter g_ble_int_count that ESP32 uses today) and no chip feature, and the legacy adapter has no nesting guard of any kind, while the ESP32 and ESP32-S3 adapters and the newer ESP32-C3 adapter arch/risc-v/src/esp32c3/esp_ble_adapter.c all keep one. The legacy OSI table also uses the same OSI_VERSION 0x00010006 as the ESP32-S3 adapter that received the same fix (commit 6521bdfa1). Confidence is medium because whether the binary legacy ESP32-C3 controller library really nests these calls cannot be seen in the repository.
same_problem_note: Same saved-interrupt-state global in esp32c3_ble_adapter.c as nuttx-180: the same fix was made in the ESP32-S3 BLE adapter on 2023-10-05 and in the ESP32 adapter on 2023-11-10.

title: bl808 map_region() builds wrong page tables when a region does not start on a 2 MiB boundary
summary: In June 2025 qemu-rv fixed map_region() so that each L3 page table is filled only up to the next 2 MiB (section) boundary before the next table is looked up; before that, a region with an unaligned start wrapped around inside one table, overwriting earlier entries and leaving the following range unmapped. bl808_mm_init.c still has the old loop, which maps up to 512 pages into one table regardless of where vaddr starts. Today the ox64 linker script puts kernel text at 0x50200000 and kernel data at 0x50400000, each 2 MiB, so nothing goes wrong in the in-tree configuration. A board or linker-script change that starts kernel text or data off a 2 MiB boundary would silently get broken kernel mappings; note that the L3 pool (PGT_L3_SIZE, two tables) would also need to grow for unaligned regions, as qemu-rv did.

fix.subject: risc-v/mmu: Fix map_region() for incorrect page table setup when vaddr is unaligned

evidence: The fix rewrites map_region() in qemu_rv_mm_init.c so that the inner loop stops at the next section boundary (ALIGN_UP_MASK(vaddr + 1, RV_MMU_SECTION_ALIGN_MASK)) and the outer loop runs while vaddr < endaddr; the commit message says an unaligned vaddr "causes incorrect address mapping for later regions". map_region() in bl808_mm_init.c (line 186) still has the identical pre-fix loops (lines 197, 200, 221): it looks up one L3 table for vaddr and then writes up to RV_MMU_PAGE_ENTRIES entries into it, while mmu_ln_setentry() picks the slot only from the vaddr bits (riscv_mmu.c line 130), so a region that starts off a 2 MiB boundary wraps into the wrong slots of that table and the next 2 MiB never gets its own table. BL808 is SV39-only (arch/risc-v/Kconfig line 471) and both macros the fix uses exist for it (RV_MMU_SECTION_ALIGN_MASK in riscv_mmu.h line 127, ALIGN_UP_MASK in include/nuttx/nuttx.h line 55), so nothing on this side makes the fix inapplicable. However, the only in-tree board (ox64 ld.script lines 25-26) puts kflash and ksram at 2 MiB-aligned origins with 2 MiB lengths, so the calls at lines 274 and 278 never pass an unaligned start today and the defect is latent.

title: LiteX map_region() still builds wrong kernel page tables when a region does not start on a 4 MiB boundary.
summary: In June 2025 the QEMU RISC-V port fixed map_region() (commit 6a9a835d) so that it fills each leaf page table only up to the next section boundary and keeps going until the end address, because an unaligned start address gave wrong mappings for later addresses. The LiteX copy of map_region() still has the old loops: it writes up to 1024 entries into the table found for the start address, so for a region that starts inside a 4 MiB block, the entries meant for the next block wrap around into the start of the current table, overwrite the mappings there, and the next block is left without a table. The in-tree arty_a7 kernel linker script places kernel text, kernel data and the page pool on 4 MiB boundaries, so current in-tree builds do not reach this path; a LiteX board or linker script with an unaligned region would boot with corrupted kernel mappings. The loop change ports as is (plus an include of nuttx/nuttx.h); an unaligned layout may also need a larger CONFIG_LITEX_MMU_L2_SIZE, much as the QEMU commit enlarged its own table pool.

fix.subject: risc-v/mmu: Fix map_region() for incorrect page table setup when vaddr is unaligned

evidence: The hunks rewrite map_region() so that each inner loop stops at the next section boundary (ALIGN_UP_MASK(vaddr + 1, RV_MMU_SECTION_ALIGN_MASK)) and the outer loop runs until endaddr, because, in the commit message's words, 'When the vaddr parameter passed to map_region() is not aligned to the page directory, it causes incorrect address mapping for later regions.' map_region() in litex_mm_init.c (SV32 only) is the pre-fix code line for line: it counts leaf tables from npages alone (lines 172, 175) and writes up to RV_MMU_PAGE_ENTRIES entries into the single table pbase found for the starting vaddr (lines 196-198), and mmu_ln_setentry() indexes with (vaddr >> shift) & RV_MMU_VPN_MASK (riscv_mmu.c line 130), so a region that starts off a 4 MiB boundary wraps into the wrong table and the outer loop can stop one table short. title: S32K1xx LPUART TX DMA marks the wrapped part of the TX buffer as sent although it was never transmitted when scatter/gather descriptors are not configured.
summary: In September 2026 (commit 6b0f85b7) the i.MX RT LPUART driver was changed to queue and count the wrapped second part of the TX ring buffer only when CONFIG_IMXRT_EDMA_NTCD > 1, that is, only when scatter/gather descriptors exist. The S32K1xx LPUART driver has the same TX DMA code: it always tries to queue the second part and its completion callback always reports both parts as sent. With the default CONFIG_S32K1XX_EDMA_NTCD=0 the eDMA driver refuses the second part with -EBUSY, so only the first part is transmitted, yet the serial layer frees both, and any write whose data wraps around the end of the TX buffer silently loses the wrapped bytes. This only affects builds that enable LPUART TX DMA (CONFIG_LPUARTn_TXDMA), which no in-tree s32k1xx defconfig does. The fix is the same NTCD guard in s32k1xx_dma_txcallback() and s32k1xx_dma_send(), plus restarting the next transfer from the callback so the remaining bytes do not wait for the next write.

title: S32K3xx LPUART TX DMA still queues and counts the wrapped second segment even when no scatter/gather descriptors are configured.
summary: In September 2026 (commit 6b0f85b7) the i.MX RT LPUART driver was changed to queue and count the wrapped second part of the TX ring buffer only when CONFIG_IMXRT_EDMA_NTCD > 1, because without in-memory descriptors the second part overwrites the first and the serial buffer is advanced past unsent data. The S32K3xx LPUART driver has the same TX DMA code, unchanged: it always queues the second part and always reports both parts as sent. With the default CONFIG_S32K3XX_EDMA_NTCD=32 this works through scatter/gather, but a build that sets it to 0 (allowed by the Kconfig help, to disable in-memory descriptors) sends only the second part and drops the first whenever TX data wraps, and a build with 1 blocks waiting for a second descriptor. The fix ports with only the config symbol renamed, in both s32k3xx_dma_txcallback() and s32k3xx_dma_send().

title: S32K1xx LPSPI DMA exchange counts 4 bytes per 16-bit word, so 9-16-bit transfers overrun the caller's buffers.
summary: In October 2024 the i.MX9 LPSPI driver fixed its DMA exchange for 9-16-bit words: it now counts 2 bytes per word instead of 4 and programs the DMA with the number of words instead of that byte count. The S32K1xx LPSPI DMA exchange is the same older code: it still counts 4 bytes per word and uses that count as the number of 16-bit DMA items, while the DMA reads and writes the caller's buffers directly. A 9-16-bit SPI exchange on a DMA-enabled LPSPI therefore clocks out four times as many frames, reads past the end of the TX buffer and writes past the end of the RX buffer, corrupting memory. The same three-line change applies here unchanged (the byte count plus the two config.iter lines); changing only the byte count would still leave the DMA moving twice the requested words.
