title: ESP32-C3 (legacy) SPI polling exchange copies whole 4-byte words past the end of buffers whose length is not a multiple of 4.
summary: In February 2026 the ESP32 SPI driver fixed esp32_spi_poll_exchange() so that each memcpy() copies only the bytes left in the transfer instead of always 4, because 1-byte and other unaligned transfers were reading and writing past the caller's buffers and smashing the stack. The ESP32-C3 legacy driver's esp32c3_spi_poll_exchange() is the same code and still copies 4 bytes per data register in both the transmit and receive loops. Any polled exchange whose length is not a multiple of 4 bytes (every such exchange without SPI DMA, and the short ones with it) writes up to 3 bytes past the end of the receive buffer and reads up to 3 bytes past the transmit buffer, which can corrupt the stack or neighbouring data. The fix ports unchanged: take the chunk as the smaller of 4 and the bytes left, and use it for both copies and pointer steps.

title: AT32 PWM stop does not clear the channel compare registers, so a channel can come back with its old duty after a stop.
summary: In February 2024 the STM32 PWM driver started zeroing the four channel compare registers (CCR1-CCR4) in pwm_stop(), because after a STOP in multichannel mode a channel was still outputting; the same lines are now also in the STM32F7, H7 and H5 drivers. The AT32 PWM driver, which was copied from the STM32 driver, still only stops the counter and disables the outputs, leaving the old duty values in place. Because a later start rewrites the duty only of the channels it lists but re-enables every configured output, a channel that is not listed in the next start comes back with its previous duty instead of staying off. The fix ports by renaming the register offsets to AT32_GTIM_CCRx_OFFSET; the commit does not explain the exact STOP symptom, so the restart case above is the effect that can be confirmed from the code.

fix.subject: arch/stm32: Clear all PWM channel when during STOP

evidence: The hunk adds four writes to pwm_stop() that zero CCR1-CCR4 after the counter and outputs are disabled; the commit message says 'I noticed when executing pwm STOP command in multichannel mode, the channel still outputting. This commit fixes this issue.' at32_pwm.c is a copy of the STM32 driver and its pwm_stop() is the pre-fix code: it disables the counter and the configured outputs (lines 3724-3726) and leaves every compare register as it was, and nothing else in the file clears them (the only CCR write is pwm_ccr_update() called from pwm_duty_update(), line 2097). The visible restart path shows why the stale values matter: pwm_timer() rewrites the duty only for channels listed in the request (pwm_duty_channels_update() skips channel 0 and stops at -1, lines 3139-3149) but then re-enables every board-configured output (lines 3260-3264), so a channel left out of the next start comes back with its old duty; the commit itself does not say why disabling the outputs was not enough, which is why confidence is medium. The fix needs only AT32_GTIM_CCR1_OFFSET to AT32_GTIM_CCR4_OFFSET, which hardware/at32_tim.h defines, and the same block is also present in the STM32F7, STM32H7 and STM32H5 PWM drivers.

title: The AT32 SPI DMA exchange does not split requests larger than the 16-bit DMA transfer count and does not shrink nwords when the copy is clipped to the driver buffer.
summary: Upstream commit 8302295dd018 (2026-05-15) changed the STM32 SPI driver to run DMA exchanges in chunks of at most 65535 words and to shrink nwords when the copy into the driver's own DMA buffer is clipped to buflen. The AT32 copy in at32_spi.c still hands the full nwords to spi_dmarxsetup()/spi_dmatxsetup() and on to at32_dmasetup(), whose only guard is a debug assertion before the value is written into the CNDTR register, and it then waits for the DMA callback with no timeout. An exchange of 65536 words or more therefore trips the assertion in debug builds and otherwise programs a truncated count, which per the STM32 commit hangs the caller (for an exact 64 Ki-word transfer) or silently exchanges fewer words than requested. When an in-driver DMA buffer is configured and the request is larger than it, the DMA is still programmed with the unclipped nwords and can run past that buffer. The fix has to be adapted so that each chunk keeps the SPIEN disable/enable steps that the AT32 version performs around the DMA setup.

fix.subject: arch/arm/src/stm32/stm32_spi: chunk DMA exchanges to honor 16-bit NDTR

evidence: The second picked hunk is the real fix of commit 8302295dd018 ("chunk DMA exchanges to honor 16-bit NDTR"): spi_exchange() forwarded the caller's full nwords to the DMA setup, so an exchange of 65536 words or more programmed a truncated count and "the caller deadlocked in spi_dmarxwait()"; it also rescales nwords after nbytes is clipped to priv->buflen (the first hunk only adds declarations, a %zu format and a comment typo fix). The DMA spi_exchange() in at32_spi.c has the same pre-fix code: it clips nbytes to priv->buflen without touching nwords (lines 1575-1577) and calls spi_dmarxsetup()/spi_dmatxsetup() with the full nwords (lines 1587-1588), which pass it unchanged to at32_dmasetup() (lines 802-803). The AT32 DMA setup only has DEBUGASSERT(ntransfers < 65536), the same check as the STM32 IPv1 DMAMUX driver (common/stm32/stm32_dma_m3m4_v1_8ch_dmamux.c line 735), and then writes ntransfers into the CNDTR register, while spi_dmarxwait() loops on nxsem_wait_uninterruptible() until the DMA callback sets rxresult, with no timeout. Nothing else splits or rejects large requests (at32_dmacapable() checks only alignment and memory region), and the AT32_SPI_DMA and AT32_SPI1_DMA_BUFFER options exist, so both the oversized-count case and the clipped-buffer case apply; the only structural difference is the SPIEN disable/enable around the DMA setup (lines 1585 and 1613), which a chunk loop must keep.

title: The GD32VW55x SPI DMA exchange puts the whole request into a 16-bit DMA count, so exchanges of 65536 or more words are silently truncated.
summary: In May 2026 apache/nuttx commit 8302295dd0 made the STM32 SPI driver split DMA exchanges into chunks of at most 65535 words, because the DMA transfer count is 16 bits wide and an exact 64 KiB exchange left the caller blocked in spi_dmarxwait(). The GD32VW55x SPI driver, added in July 2026 with the same structure, still sets up a single DMA transfer with the caller's nwords, which is truncated to 16 bits when stored in the uint16_t number field and written to the 16-bit CHCNT counter. An exchange of 65536 or more words therefore moves the wrong number of words, and for exactly 65536 words the count becomes zero, which on STM32 caused a hang; whether a zero count hangs on this chip as well cannot be confirmed from the repository. The fix has to be rewritten for gd32_dma_setup() (a loop over chunks that advances the buffer pointers), since this driver has no bounce buffer; the fix commit notes that 'Single-descriptor transfers (every in-tree caller today) are byte-for-byte identical', so the problem shows only for exchanges of 65536 or more words.

fix.subject: arch/arm/src/stm32/stm32_spi: chunk DMA exchanges to honor 16-bit NDTR

evidence: The matched lines 1190-1191 are in the DMA spi_exchange() of gd32vw55x_spi.c, which follows the pre-fix STM32 code step by step: one RX/TX DMA setup with the caller's full nwords, then the same SPI_TRIGGER/start/wait sequence. spi_dmarxsetup()/spi_dmatxsetup() store nwords in dma_init_struct.number (lines 1044 and 1098), which is a uint16_t field in gd32vw55x_dma.h, and gd32vw55x_dma.c writes it into CHCNT, whose counter is 'Bits 0-15' in hardware/gd32vw55x_dma.h; so an exchange of 65536 or more words is silently cut to its low 16 bits, the same problem the commit describes ('silently programmed NDTR to (nwords & 0xffff)'). title: nuc1xx up_prioritize_irq() writes the PendSV and SysTick priorities into SHPR2 instead of SHPR3, so a SysTick request changes the SVCall priority instead.
summary: On 2025-04-16 commit 8ac09bcf fixed rp23xx up_prioritize_irq() so that PendSV and SysTick priorities go to System Handler Priority Register 3 (0xe000ed20) instead of SHPR2 (0xe000ed1c); that code had been copied from the ARMv6-M rp2040 driver. The nuc1xx copy still uses ARMV6M_SYSCON_SHPR2 with the SHPR3 field shifts, although its own armv6-m header places PendSV and SysTick in SHPR3 and SVCall in SHPR2 bits 24-31, and its timer code already uses SHPR3 for SysTick. With CONFIG_ARCH_IRQPRIO enabled, asking for a new SysTick priority silently changes the SVCall priority, asking for a new PendSV priority writes unused SHPR2 bits, and in both cases the requested priority never takes effect although the function returns OK. Only the register part of the fix applies (use ARMV6M_SYSCON_SHPR3 in both branches); the rename to ARMv8-M macro names does not, and nothing in arch/arm/src/nuc1xx or arch/arm/src/armv6-m calls this function, so the problem only shows when board or application code reprioritizes PendSV or SysTick.

fix.subject: arch/arm/rp23xx: Fix IRQ prioritize

evidence: The commit message says it "Fixes the reg addresses that were copied from armv6 rp2040 to the actual armv8 spec", but only the second hunk changes behaviour: the first hunk swaps ARMV6M_NVIC_IPR(irq >> 2) for NVIC_IRQ_PRIORITY(irq), which give the same address (0xe000e400 + 4*(irq >> 2) by armv6-m/nvic.h and armv8-m/nvic.h), so it is only a rename that ARMv6-M code does not need, while the second hunk moves the PendSV and SysTick writes from SHPR2 (0xe000ed1c) to NVIC_SYSH12_15_PRIORITY (0xe000ed20, "System handler 12-15 priority register") with the same shift values 16 and 24. In nuc1xx up_prioritize_irq() (nuc_irq.c 347-356, built with CONFIG_ARCH_IRQPRIO, which this chip can enable because ARCH_CHIP_NUC1XX selects ARCH_CORTEXM0 and that selects ARCH_HAVE_IRQPRIO) the PendSV and SysTick branches are the same pre-fix lines, still writing ARMV6M_SYSCON_SHPR2 with SYSCON_SHPR3_PRI_14_SHIFT / SYSCON_SHPR3_PRI_15_SHIFT. The armv6-m/nvic.h that nuc_irq.c includes as "nvic.h" puts PendSV (bits 16-23) and SysTick (bits 24-31) in System handler priority register 3 at offset 0x0020 and gives SHPR2 only the SVCall field in bits 24-31, and nuc_timerisr.c itself sets the SysTick priority through ARMV6M_SYSCON_SHPR3. So the register error is not specific to ARMv8: a SysTick request rewrites the SVCall priority, which the function comment says must not be modified, and neither the PendSV nor the SysTick priority changes; the other ARMv6-M copies (rp2040, kl, samd2l2) carry the same lines, so none shows a different handling.

title: s32k1xx LPUART TX DMA leaves bytes that were queued during a running transfer unsent until the next write.
summary: On 2023-12-05 s32k3xx_serial.c dropped its TX DMA semaphore and made the DMA completion callback restart DMA whenever the transmit buffer still holds data, fixing stuttering output caused by the earlier switch to nxsem_trywait. s32k1xx_serial.c received that same trywait switch in November 2023 but still has the old code: its completion callback only posts txdmasem, and s32k1xx_dma_txavailable silently skips sending when the trywait fails. Data written while a TX DMA transfer is in flight therefore stays in the transmit buffer until some later write, drain or echo calls dmatxavail again, so serial or console output can stall or arrive in bursts. Porting also needs the matching eDMA change: an idle-check function and marking the channel idle before the callback runs in s32k1xx_dmaterminate.

fix.subject: s32k3xx:Serial refactor out tx dma semaphore

evidence: The picked hunks fix a runtime bug: the message says that after the TX DMA semaphore 'was switched to trywait in 8362e314, it left data in the xmit queue unsent', and the fix makes the DMA completion callback call s32k3xx_dma_txavailable to send remaining data and makes txavailable test s32k3xx_dmach_idle instead of the semaphore. s32k1xx_dma_txcallback (lines 1735-1753) and s32k1xx_dma_txavailable (lines 1764-1777) are the same pre-fix logic line for line: the callback only calls uart_xmitchars_done and nxsem_post, and txavailable starts a transfer only when nxsem_trywait succeeds; s32k1xx received the same trywait change in a92bd5d08 ('s32k1xx:Serial Do not wait on TXDMA semaphore', 2023-11-10). At the pinned commit the serial upper half (drivers/serial/serial.c, serial_dma.c) calls dmatxavail only from write, drain and echo paths, uart_xmitchars_done and uart_datasent only advance the tail and wake waiters, and s32k1xx_dma_txint does nothing, so bytes queued while a transfer is running stay in the buffer until a later write. The port must be adapted: s32k1xx_edma.c has no dmach_idle function, and s32k1xx_dmaterminate invokes the callback (line 494) before setting S32K1XX_DMA_IDLE (line 499), the ordering s32k3xx changed in the companion commit 7f0643de6 ('edma clear state before callback add idle check'), so an idle check made inside the callback needs that change as well.

title: The rp2040 PWM driver still has the old divider and duty-cycle formulas and the removed info[0].duty field access that were fixed in both rp23xx PWM drivers.
summary: The ARM rp23xx PWM driver was fixed on 2026-05-25 (commit 53ef7c063) and the RISC-V rp23xx-rv copy on 2026-06-24 (commit 970f2f22): the clock divider is now a clamped 8.4 fixed-point value, the compare value is duty * (top + 1) / 65535 clamped to top, and pwm_start reads info->channels[0].duty. arch/arm/src/rp2040/rp2040_pwm.c still has the identical old code in pwm_start, setup_period and setup_pulse. If it is not fixed, a single-channel build (PWM_NCHANNELS=1, the Kconfig default) does not compile because struct pwm_info_s has no duty member, and at run time any frequency that forces top below 0xffff gives a wrongly scaled compare value (wrong duty cycle, for most duties above top, and in two-channel mode corrupting channel B), while the divider can be written outside the 0x10..0xFFF range. The patch can be carried over by renaming the rp23xx identifiers to rp2040 ones; this is based on reading the code only, not on hardware tests.

title: The cxd56 SPI driver waits for DMA completion with no timeout, so a DMA transfer that never finishes hangs the caller forever.
summary: On 2026-10-13 the rp23xx SPI driver (ARM and RISC-V ports) changed spi_dmatrxwait() to wait for the TX and RX DMA completions with nxsem_tickwait_uninterruptible() and a timeout derived from the transfer size and SPI clock, and on timeout to stop both DMA channels, reset the semaphore and drain the RX FIFO. The cxd56xx SPI driver still has the pre-fix version: two untimed uninterruptible waits on dmasem that only the DMA completion callbacks post. If a DMA transfer never finishes, the calling thread blocks forever while it holds the SPI bus lock and the PM frequency lock taken in spi_dmaexchange(), so other users of that bus stall too. The repository does not show that a DMA transfer can actually stall on the CXD56 DMA controller; that scenario comes only from the rp23xx commit message.

fix.subject: arch/rp23xx: add bounded timeout to SPI DMA completion wait

evidence: The rp23xx commit replaces the two untimed nxsem_wait_uninterruptible() calls in spi_dmatrxwait() with nxsem_tickwait_uninterruptible() bounded by a transfer-size-derived timeout, and on timeout stops both DMA channels, resets the semaphore and drains the RX FIFO; its message says "If a DMA transfer never completes (e.g. stalled slave or bus glitch), the calling thread sleeps indefinitely." cxd56_spi.c has the same spi_dmatrxwait() as the pre-fix rp23xx code: two untimed uninterruptible waits on priv->dmasem, which only spi_dmatxcallback()/spi_dmarxcallback() post, followed by cxd56_dmastop() on both channels and clearing DMACR; it is called from spi_dmaexchange() after up_pm_acquire_freqlock(), so a stuck wait also keeps the frequency lock (the flagged lines 1547/1569 are only the similar-looking spierr calls inside the DMA callbacks). Nothing in this driver bounds the wait, and everything the fix uses exists here: the frequency, actual and nbits fields, cxd56_dmastop(), the SR/RNE and DR registers for draining the RX FIFO, and the OS calls nxsem_tickwait_uninterruptible() and nxsem_reset(). The only basis for a DMA transfer that never completes is the rp23xx commit message, and the CXD56 DMA controller is different hardware, so confidence is medium.

title: The STM32WL5 serial driver computes the LPUART1 baud divisor from PCLK2, although LPUART1 is clocked from APB1 (PCLK1).
summary: On 2024-11-07 the STM32H5 serial driver fixed LPUART1 (and three USARTs) whose apbclock had been left at the default PCLK2 instead of the clock of the bus the port is on. The STM32WL5 serial driver still sets LPUART1's apbclock to STM32_PCLK2_FREQUENCY and uses it for the baud divisor, while its own clock-enable code, RCC header and early console code all treat LPUART1 as an APB1/PCLK1 peripheral. On a board whose APB1 and APB2 prescalers differ, the serial driver would program a wrong LPUART1 baud rate that also disagrees with what the early console set up. The change has to be adapted: on WL5 the value should be STM32_PCLK1_FREQUENCY, not PCLK3. The only in-tree board runs PCLK1 and PCLK2 at the same 48 MHz, so no in-tree configuration shows the error today.

The only in-tree board, nucleo-wl55jc, sets PCLK1 and PCLK2 both to HCLK/1 (board.h lines 87 and 99), so the error has no visible effect there today.
impact_note: The only in-tree STM32WL5 board (nucleo-wl55jc) sets PCLK1 and PCLK2 both to HCLK/1, so the divisor comes out the same today; only a board with different APB1 and APB2 prescalers would get a wrong LPUART1 baud rate.

title: The ESP32-C3 BLE adapter's esp_update_time() can leave tv_nsec at one second or more, so timed BLE message-queue sends and receives fail with EINVAL.
summary: On 2024-10-07, commit b3727f67bee3 rewrote esp_update_time() in the ESP32, ESP32-S3 and legacy ESP32-C3 BLE and Wi-Fi adapters to use clock_ticks2time() and clock_timespec_add(), which carry nanoseconds above one second into tv_sec. The newer ESP32-C3 BLE adapter (arch/risc-v/src/esp32c3/esp_ble_adapter.c) still has the old body, even though esp_wifi_adapter.c in the same directory has the fixed one. Whenever the current time's nanoseconds plus the timeout's fraction of a second reach one second, file_mq_timedsend() and file_mq_timedreceive() reject the deadline with -EINVAL, so a timed BLE queue send fails and a timed receive returns at once instead of waiting. This is the same failure the commit reports for Wi-Fi scanning, and the two-line fix can be copied as is.

fix.subject: esp32: fix esp32 wifi bug caused scan failed

evidence: The fix replaced the hand-written body of esp_update_time() with clock_ticks2time() plus clock_timespec_add(), because, in the commit's words, "mq_timedsend() return failed because the time valid check error. the ts_nsec is bigger than 1000000000. esp_update_time() hasn't consider of the ns > 1s after the adding calculation". In arch/risc-v/src/esp32c3/esp_ble_adapter.c, esp_update_time() (lines 2198-2209) is still the exact pre-fix body: it adds TICK2NSEC() of the leftover ticks to timespec->tv_nsec with no carry into tv_sec. It is used the same way as on the fixed side: queue_recv_wrapper() and esp_queue_send_generic() take clock_gettime(CLOCK_REALTIME), call esp_update_time() and pass the result to file_mq_timedreceive()/file_mq_timedsend(), which at the pinned commit return -EINVAL when abstime->tv_nsec >= 1000000000 (sched/mqueue/mq_send.c line 305, sched/mqueue/mq_receive.c line 163). Nothing chip- or config-specific stands in the way: the sibling arch/risc-v/src/esp32c3/esp_wifi_adapter.c in the same directory already has the fixed esp_update_time() using clock_ticks2time()/clock_timespec_add(), and the BLE adapter is built whenever CONFIG_ESPRESSIF_BLE is set.

title: imxrt EHCI transfer cancellation tests for the target QH the wrong way round, so a cancelled in-progress transfer is never removed from the schedule.
summary: On 2024-01-20 commit bca8df7d fixed two reversed tests in sama5's EHCI transfer cancellation: sam_qh_cancel() now skips QHs that belong to other endpoints, and sam_cancel() skips the search only when the asynchronous queue is empty. imxrt_ehci.c has the same cancellation code and still has both pre-fix tests: imxrt_qh_cancel() treats the matching QH as 'keep looking' (line 3149), and imxrt_cancel() reports success without searching whenever the queue holds any QH (line 4846). As the sama5 commit message describes, cancelling a bulk or control transfer that is still in progress then leaves its QH linked in the schedule, and later communication with the device fails (the sama5 fix was checked with the CDC-ACM driver and the cu command). The listed hunk is a one-operator change, but the companion test at line 4846 must be flipped as well (with priv->asynchead in place of &g_asynchead) for the search to run at all.

fix.subject: arm: sama5: sam_ehci: fix transfer cancellation process.

evidence: The sama5 commit 'arm: sama5: sam_ehci: fix transfer cancellation process.' says 'The logic of the conditional expression that determines whether the QH is a target QH or not is reversed in the process of canceling a transfer in INPROGRESS state' and that therefore 'the QH in INPROGRESS state is not released and subsequent communication is not successful'; the listed hunk flips sam_qh_cancel()'s test to 'if (qh->epinfo != epinfo)' (sam_ehci.c line 2724). imxrt_ehci.c line 3149 is in imxrt_qh_cancel(), the same imxrt_qh_foreach() callback that imxrt_cancel() passes at line 4900, and it still returns OK under the comment 'No... keep looking' when qh->epinfo == epinfo, so it skips the QH being cancelled and would unlink and free a non-matching one instead. The companion test that the same commit flipped in sam_cancel() (sam_ehci.c line 4446) is also still pre-fix here, written with the per-controller head: 'if (qh && qh != priv->asynchead)' at line 4846 claims success without searching whenever the asynchronous queue is not empty. Nothing the fix relies on is missing: QHs record their epinfo (line 1894), imxrt_qh_cancel() is built under CONFIG_USBHOST_ASYNCH (line 3131), which IMXRT_USBOTG1 selects (arch/arm/src/imxrt/Kconfig line 571), and the change is plain C logic with no register dependence.

title: The nRF53 SPI driver uses NRF53_SPIM4_BASE unconditionally, so a network-core build with SPI0 enabled fails to compile.
summary: In March 2024 the nrf91 SPI driver was fixed to build by removing the SPIM4 exception from the >8 MHz frequency limit, because nRF91 has no SPIM4. The nrf53 copy still has the same check at line 787 in nrf53_spi_setfrequency(); it is correct on the nRF5340 application core, which has SPIM4, but the network-core memory map defines only SPIM0 while Kconfig still lets SPI0 be enabled there. In that configuration the driver would fail to compile on an undefined NRF53_SPIM4_BASE, the same error nrf91 had. No in-tree network-core board config enables SPI, so the problem is latent, and the fix has to be a conditional guard rather than the nrf91 deletion. This comes from reading Kconfig and headers only; no network-core build was tried.

fix.subject: arch/nrf91: fix compilation for SPI

evidence: The nrf91 commit "fix compilation for SPI" ("remove references to unsupported SPI freq and SPI4 which is not supported") drops the SPIM4 exception from the >8 MHz limit in setfrequency because NRF91_SPIM4_BASE does not exist on that chip. nrf53_spi_setfrequency() line 787 has the same pre-fix check; on the nRF5340 application core it is correct and needed (NRF53_SPIM4_BASE is defined in nrf53_memorymap_cpuapp.h, the driver has a g_spi4dev instance, SPIM_FREQUENCY_16MBPS/32MBPS exist), so the nrf91 deletion itself must not be copied. But the same driver also builds for the network core: Kconfig offers NRF53_SPI0_MASTER outside "if NRF53_HAVE_SPI1234" (selected only by NRF53_APPCORE), nrf53_memorymap.h then includes nrf53_memorymap_cpunet.h, which defines only NRF53_SPIM0_BASE, and line 787 is under no #ifdef (the only other SPIM4 use, line 394, is inside CONFIG_NRF53_SPI4_MASTER). A net-core build with SPI0 enabled would therefore hit the same undefined SPIM4-base compile error the nrf91 commit fixed; no in-tree *_cpunet defconfig enables SPI, so it is latent, and the adapted fix is a guard (for example on CONFIG_NRF53_SPI4_MASTER) rather than deleting the check.
impact_note: It is only a compile failure, and only for a network-core configuration with SPI0 enabled, which no in-tree board config uses; application-core builds compile and run unchanged.

title: The at32 SocketCAN transmit path asserts that an extended CAN ID, still carrying the EFF flag, is below 2^29, which always fails for extended frames.
summary: In October 2024 the stm32 and stm32f7 SocketCAN drivers changed the extended-ID assertion to drop CAN_EFF_FLAG before comparing against 2^29. The at32 copy still asserts frame->can_id < (1 << 29) inside the branch that requires CAN_EFF_FLAG, so with debug assertions on, sending any extended-ID frame would stop the system. Right now this is masked because the same CONFIG_NET_CAN_EXTID block also uses CAN_TIR_EXID_MASK, which at32 does not define, so extended-ID support does not build on at32; whoever fixes that build error will hit the assertion next. The STM32 one-line change applies unchanged.

fix.subject: arch/arm/stm32{|f7}/socketcan: fix debugassert for extid frames

evidence: The stm32/stm32f7 commit says "fix debugassert for extid frames, we have to remove CAN_EFF_FLAG bit from the expression": inside "if (frame->can_id & CAN_EFF_FLAG)" the ID always carries CAN_EFF_FLAG (0x80000000 in include/nuttx/can.h), so "frame->can_id < (1 << 29)" can never hold and the assertion fires on every extended-ID frame when debug assertions are enabled. at32can_transmit() in at32_can_sock.c has exactly the same branch and assertion at line 892, followed by the same bxCAN-style ID write (ID shifted by CAN_TMI_TMEID_SHIFT plus the ID-type bit), and nothing chip-specific is involved: CAN_EFF_FLAG is already used on line 890 and the corrected expression needs nothing else. Separately, the same CONFIG_NET_CAN_EXTID block uses CAN_TIR_EXID_MASK on line 889, which no header reachable from at32 defines (only STM32 hardware headers do), and the only in-tree at32 socket config (at32f437-mini can_socket) does not enable NET_CAN_EXTID, so this path does not build today and the bug is masked. Once extended-ID support is made to build on at32, the wrong assertion would trip on the first extended frame; the STM32 one-line change can be copied unchanged.
impact_note: DEBUGASSERT is only active in debug-assertion builds, and on at32 the extended-ID block currently does not compile (line 889 uses an STM32-only macro), so no working build reaches this line today.

title: The SAMA5 MCAN debug check in mcan_txready() can fire falsely when the TX FIFO frees a slot before the TX-complete interrupt has posted the semaphore.
summary: In September 2026 the samv7 MCAN driver relaxed the debug assertion in mcan_txready() so that it only checks that the semaphore count does not exceed the FIFO size, because the hardware can report a free TX FIFO slot before the interrupt handler has incremented txfsem. The sama5 MCAN driver has the same code and still asserts that the FIFO-not-full flag and the semaphore count agree. With CONFIG_DEBUG_FEATURES and debug assertions enabled, keeping the CAN TX queue full (for example when sending large data) can make the assertion fire and halt the system although nothing is wrong. Release builds are not affected, and the samv7 change can be copied as is.

fix.subject: arch/arm/src/samv7/sam_mcan.c: fix potential false debug assertions

changes.diff:
#ifdef CONFIG_DEBUG_FEATURES
   /* As a sanity check, the txfsem should also track the number of elements
-   * the TX FIFO/queue.  Make sure that they are consistent.
+   * the TX FIFO/queue. Check only if the value doesn't exceed number of
+   * FIFO queue members. Sanity check comparing semaphore value with notfull
+   * flag may not always work, because SAM_MCAN_TXFQS register may signalize
+   * not full queue before we process the interrupt and increment the
+   * semaphore. The sanity checks should not be necessary because
+   * mcan_buffer_reserve function will take care of fixing the semaphore
+   * value if it doesn't match with the FIFO.
+   *
+   * REVISIT: The entire semaphore logic is a bit weird and probably not
+   * necessary. All we need to do is to check SAM_MCAN_TXFQS register
+   * if there is at least one free slot in the queue.
    */
 
   nxsem_get_value(&priv->txfsem, &sval);
-  DEBUGASSERT(((notfull && sval > 0) || (!notfull && sval <= 0)) &&
-              (sval <= priv->config->ntxfifoq));
+  DEBUGASSERT((sval <= priv->config->ntxfifoq));
 #endif
 
   nxmutex_unlock(&priv->lock);

evidence: The samv7 commit explains that the TX FIFO can be "not full but the semaphore is not yet incremented because the driver didn't handle the interrupt", which "leads to the debug assertion", and that "mcan_buffer_reserve function will take care of fixing the semaphore value if it doesn't match with the FIFO"; it therefore drops the notfull/sval consistency part of the DEBUGASSERT in mcan_txready(). sama5's mcan_txready() (line 3162) has the identical pre-fix block: it reads SAM_MCAN_TXFQS, derives notfull from MCAN_TXFQS_TFQF, and asserts ((notfull && sval > 0) || (!notfull && sval <= 0)) at lines 3195-3196 under CONFIG_DEBUG_FEATURES. The same race exists there: txfsem is posted only by mcan_buffer_release(), which mcan_interrupt() calls on TX completion (line 3838), and sama5's mcan_buffer_reserve() has the same resynchronisation (nxsem_reset to 0 or to the FIFO free level) that the commit relies on. Nothing in the change is SAMv7-specific (same register, same bit, same semaphore and config field), so the false assertion can also trigger on sama5 under sustained CAN TX load in debug builds.
impact_note: The check is compiled only with CONFIG_DEBUG_FEATURES and halts only builds with debug assertions enabled; release builds behave the same, and the commit itself says "technically it's not a big issue".

title: The EFM32 USB device driver uses an undeclared variable privep in its DMA buffer alloc/free functions, so it fails to build with USB DMA and USB tracing enabled.
summary: In October 2023 the stm32 OTG HS device driver fixed its allocbuffer/freebuffer functions, which referred to a local variable privep that is never declared, by casting the ep argument instead. The efm32 USB device driver has the same two functions with the same undeclared privep at lines 4389 and 4410. With CONFIG_USBDEV_DMA and either USB tracing or USB debug output enabled, usbtrace() is a real call and efm32_usbdev.c stops compiling; without tracing the bad expression is dropped by the macro. The stm32 change can be copied with only the struct name changed to efm32_ep_s.
evidence: The commit message is only "Fix #11005"; its two hunks replace the undeclared local "privep" in stm32_ep_allocbuffer()/stm32_ep_freebuffer() with "((struct stm32_ep_s *)ep)->epphy", which is a build fix: neither function declares privep. efm32_ep_allocbuffer() (line 4387) and efm32_ep_freebuffer() (line 4408) are the same CONFIG_USBDEV_DMA functions and still use privep->epphy at lines 4389 and 4410 with no privep declared (privep appears only as a parameter name of other functions); the neighbouring efm32_ep_freereq() already uses the correct cast form at line 4374. The error appears whenever usbtrace() is a real function, i.e. with CONFIG_USBDEV_TRACE or CONFIG_DEBUG_FEATURES plus CONFIG_DEBUG_USB (include/nuttx/usb/usbdev_trace.h); otherwise the macro discards its arguments. Nothing makes this inapplicable to efm32: USBDEV_DMA in drivers/usbdev/Kconfig depends only on USBDEV, efm32_usbdev.c wires both functions into its ops table under CONFIG_USBDEV_DMA, and struct efm32_ep_s has the epphy field.
impact_note: It only breaks compilation when CONFIG_USBDEV_DMA is combined with USB tracing or USB debug output; it does not change how a working build behaves.

title: The cxd56 USB device driver still throws away IN requests submitted while the endpoint is halted, so a mass-storage status reply can be lost.
summary: On 2026-07-28 the rp2040 and rp23xx USB device drivers stopped rejecting IN requests that arrive while an endpoint is halted: they now keep them queued and send them once the host clears the halt, because the mass storage class submits its status reply (CSW) while bulk-IN is still halted. The cxd56 driver still rejects such requests with -EBUSY in cxd56_epsubmit(), and its resume path only clears the STALL bit. The CXD56 does not declare stall queueing, so the mass storage class falls back to a 100 ms sleep workaround; if the host clears the halt later than that, the status reply is dropped and the host waits, times out and resets the device (the commit reports this with macOS). The fix has to be rewritten for this different controller, which starts IN transfers from an IN-token interrupt and can also clear the halt in hardware; how this controller treats a STALL while NAK is cleared cannot be checked from the repository.

fix.subject: rp2040/rp23xx: implement stall queueing and GET STATUS responses

evidence: The listed hunk (the same in rp2040_usbdev.c and rp23xx_usbdev.c) removes the epsubmit() branch that aborted any IN request with -EBUSY while the endpoint was halted and instead queues the request, arming it only when the endpoint is not stalled; the commit message names this as defect 1 ("epsubmit() aborted (-EBUSY) any IN request submitted while the endpoint was halted ... the CSW was dropped on the floor"), and drivers/usbdev/usbmsc_scsi.c lines 83-84 describe the same race for any controller driver. cxd56_epsubmit() still has the identical pre-fix logic: the comment at line 2416 and the branch at lines 2418-2420 abort IN requests with -EBUSY when privep->stalled is set, and only the else-branch at line 2485 enqueues; cxd56_epstall() on resume (lines 2573-2574) just clears USB_STALL and does not restart anything. ARCH_CHIP_CXD56XX (arch/arm/Kconfig line 917) does not select ARCH_USBDEV_STALLQUEUE, which the commit adds only for RP2040/RP23XX (lines 439 and 457), so usbmsc_scsi.c lines 94-95 turn on the 100 ms USBMSC_STALL_RACEWAR for cxd56 exactly as for rp23xx before the fix, and the Spresense usbmsc defconfig enables CONFIG_CXD56_USBDEV and CONFIG_USBMSC. The change cannot be copied as is: this controller starts IN transfers from the IN-token interrupt (lines 1607-1609) and can clear the halt in its hardware Clear_Feature interrupt (line 1545), and whether it keeps the STALL while NAK is cleared is not visible in the repository, so the port must be adapted and confidence is medium.

title: The RISC-V RP23xx USB device driver still throws away IN requests submitted while the endpoint is halted, so a mass-storage status reply can be lost.
summary: On 2026-07-28 the arm rp2040 and rp23xx USB device drivers were changed to keep IN requests that arrive while an endpoint is halted and send them once the host clears the halt, because the mass storage class submits its status reply (CSW) while bulk-IN is still halted. The RISC-V build of the same RP23xx chip uses its own copy of the driver, which still rejects those requests with -EBUSY in rp23xx_epsubmit() and does not restart anything when the halt clears; its chip option also does not declare stall queueing. With a host that clears the halt later than the mass storage class's 100 ms workaround allows (the commit reports macOS), the status reply is lost, the host times out and resets the device, and the volume never mounts. title: AT32 Ethernet promiscuous mode still blocks non-PAUSE control frames, so link-local multicast such as PTP may never reach the host.
summary: On 2026-09-21 the shared STM32 F1/F2/F4 Ethernet driver (stm32_eth_m3m4_v1.c, commit d357c5454) changed its promiscuous-mode frame filter to ETH_MACFFR_PCF_ALL so that all control frames are forwarded and link-local PTP multicast reaches the DMA. at32_eth.c still uses (ETH_MACFFR_PCF_PAUSE | ETH_MACFFR_PM) under CONFIG_NET_PROMISCUOUS and programs MACFFR the same way, with identical PCF definitions in its header. With promiscuous mode enabled, frames the MAC treats as control frames (per the commit, including link-local PTP multicast) are dropped before they reach the network stack or packet sockets, so L2 PTP or similar link-local protocols run over packet sockets would not receive them. Confidence is limited because AT32 has no hardware PTP support in this driver, the problem only exists with CONFIG_NET_PROMISCUOUS, and the effect on PTP frames is stated only by the commit message and the header comments, not by anything visible for this chip.

title: imx9_dmach_xfrsetup() accepts a zero iteration count and programs an eDMA transfer descriptor with CITER/BITER = 0.
summary: On 2026-10-23 the i.MX RT eDMA driver (commit d9a2e4225) made imxrt_dmach_xfrsetup() return -EINVAL when config->iter is 0, because a transfer descriptor with a zero iteration count raises the eDMA NCE error and, with Halt On Error, stops the eDMA engine. The i.MX9 copy imx9_dmach_xfrsetup() has no such check, and imx9_tcd_configure() writes config->iter straight into CITER/BITER; the i.MX95 eDMA header defines the same NCE error, and the Halt After Error option IMX9_EDMA_HOE defaults to on. On i.MX9 a zero count can arrive from the LPI2C DMA path, which uses msg->length as the count for every message including zero-length ones (the LPUART case from the original report is already guarded). Such a transfer would put the channel into an NCE error and, with the default halt-on-error setting, could make the eDMA ignore all service requests until the halt is cleared, affecting every DMA user; the exact hardware reaction is taken from the commit message and the header descriptions, and how often zero-length I2C messages are sent with DMA enabled is not visible in the repository.

fix.subject: arch/arm/imxrt: fix eDMA NCE error caused by zero-length split transfer

evidence: The selected hunk adds 'if (config->iter == 0) return -EINVAL;' to imxrt_dmach_xfrsetup(); the commit message lists it among the fixes for eDMA NCE errors, explaining that a TCD 'with iter == 0 causes eDMA NCE errors and halts the eDMA engine when HOE is enabled'. imx9_dmach_xfrsetup() in imx9_edma.c is the same function (same DEBUGASSERT/dmainfo prologue, then flags, TCD allocation and imx9_tcd_configure()), and imx9_tcd_configure() copies config->iter unchecked into tcd->citer and tcd->biter; there is no other iteration-count check in imx9_edma.c. What the fix guards against exists on i.MX9: the included imx95_edma.h defines EDMA_CH_ES_NCE ('NBYTES/CITER Configuration Error (NCE)') and EDMA_CSR_HAE ('Halt After Error'), which imx9_edma.c sets under CONFIG_IMX9_EDMA_HOE (default y). A zero count can reach the function on i.MX9: imx9_lpi2c_dma_data_configure() sets config.iter = msg->length and is called for every message that has a START command, including zero-length ones, while the LPUART split-transfer trigger named in the commit is already guarded there with nlength > 0, so only this API check is missing.

title: kinetis_dmach_xfrsetup() accepts a zero major-iteration count and programs it into the eDMA TCD instead of rejecting it.
summary: On 2026-10-23 commit d9a2e4225 made imxrt_dmach_xfrsetup() return -EINVAL when config->iter is 0, because a TCD with a zero iteration count raises the eDMA NBYTES/CITER configuration error and, with Halt On Error, stops the eDMA engine. The Kinetis eDMA driver is a copy of the same code and still writes config->iter into CITER and BITER with no check, on hardware whose headers define the same NCE error and whose Kconfig has the same HOE option, enabled by default. If a caller ever passes a zero count, the channel gets a configuration error and, with HOE, all DMA requests stop being serviced, and this driver has no code to clear HALT. No in-tree Kinetis caller passes zero today (RX DMA buffers are at least one cache line, small SPI transfers bypass DMA), so the practical risk is limited to other or future callers.

title: s32k1xx_dmach_xfrsetup() accepts a zero major-iteration count, so a zero-length DMA transfer such as a zero-length LPI2C message programs CITER=0 and can halt the eDMA.
summary: On 2026-10-23 commit d9a2e4225 made imxrt_dmach_xfrsetup() return -EINVAL when config->iter is 0, because a TCD with a zero iteration count raises the eDMA NBYTES/CITER configuration error and, with Halt On Error, stops the eDMA engine. title: The SAMA5 MCAN message RAM arrays are not kept inside one 64 KB window, although the controller only gets 16-bit buffer offsets under a single upper-16-bit base.
summary: In February 2025 (commit ef469bac) the SAMv7 MCAN driver moved its message RAM arrays into a '.mcan' section at the start of .data and zero-initialized them, because buffers lying past a 64 KB boundary were accessed at the wrong address and wrong data went out on the CAN bus. The SAMA5 copy of the driver programs the same 16-bit offsets and a single upper-16-bit base in SFR_CAN, but its g_mcan0_msgram and g_mcan1_msgram are still ordinary arrays placed wherever the linker puts them. If an array crosses a 64 KB boundary, the filters, receive FIFOs or transmit buffers after the boundary are read and written at the wrong memory address, so frames could be sent with wrong data or received into unrelated memory. The SAMv7 change cannot be copied as is, because SAMA5 linker scripts have no .mcan section and .data does not start on a 64 KB boundary there; a SAMA5-specific placement or alignment is needed. The commit notes the behaviour is not documented in the manual, so a hardware check on SAMA5 would confirm it.

#ifdef CONFIG_SAMV7_MCAN0

evidence: The picked hunks are the driver half of a real fix: SAMv7 put g_mcan0_msgram/g_mcan1_msgram into a '.mcan' section that its board linker scripts place at the start of .data (the start of SRAM, after an optional RAM vector table), because each buffer start is programmed as a 16-bit offset under one shared upper-16-bit base, and with a message RAM crossing a 64 KB boundary 'MCAN would sent data located at 0x20400000 to the network' (commit message). The SAMA5 copy uses the same addressing: MAILBOX_ADDRESS keeps only the low 16 bits (line 700), and sam_mcan_initialize() writes a single MSB taken from msgram.stdfilters into SFR_CAN (lines 4342 and 4366; hardware/sam_sfr.h line 249 'Bits 0-15: MSB CAN0 Base Address'), exactly like the SAMv7 MATRIX CAN0DMABA write. Its message RAM arrays (lines 998-1003 and 1089-1094) are still plain .bss arrays with only cache-line alignment, and nothing in the driver checks that they stay inside one 64 KB window, so the same failure can occur when the link places an array across a boundary. The fix must be adapted: no SAMA5 board linker script has a .mcan section, and e.g. sama5d2-xult uboot.ld puts .data right after .text in SDRAM, so 'start of .data' is not 64 KB aligned as SRAM start is on SAMv7; the zero-initialization part adds little because the arrays stay in .bss, which arm_data_initialize() already clears. Confidence is medium because the commit itself says the issue 'is not described anywhere in the manual' and whether a given SAMA5 image straddles a boundary depends on its layout.

title: The SAMD5E5 DMA driver declares its LPRAM descriptor tables with invalid syntax and does not compile when DMA is enabled.
summary: In November 2023 (commit f5374e71) the SAMD2L2 DMA driver changed 'locate_data(".lpram"), aligned(16);' to 'locate_data(".lpram") aligned_data(16);' to fix the build. No in-tree SAMD5E5 board configuration enables DMA, which is likely why this has not been reported.

title: The ESP32/S2/S3 I2S driver treats a sample-rate query (rate 0) as a set request and then divides by zero.
summary: The Espressif RISC-V I2S driver was refactored in October 2025 (commit fb93a9e4); among many changes, i2s_txsamplerate and i2s_rxsamplerate now return the current rate when called with rate 0, which is how the I2S character driver implements its get-sample-rate ioctls. The Xtensa common driver, which ESP32, ESP32-S2 and ESP32-S3 boards use and expose as /dev/i2scharN, still has the old code: it stops the channel, stores 0 in priv->rate and calls i2s_check_mclkfrequency, which computes priv->mclk_freq % priv->rate. A get-sample-rate ioctl on these boards therefore divides by zero (undefined behaviour, likely a crash) and in any case overwrites the configured rate with 0 after stopping the channel. Only the early return for rate 0 needs to be carried over, adapted to this driver; the matching zero handling for data width and channel count is in other hunks of the same commit, and the rest of the candidate hunks belong to the RISC-V move to the GDMA driver and do not apply. This conclusion comes from reading the code paths only; nothing was built or run.

title: S32K1xx LPSPI DMA transfers four times too many words when SPI words are wider than 8 bits.
summary: In February 2026 the i.MX RT LPSPI driver fixed its DMA exchange for words wider than 8 bits: the byte count became nwords << 1 instead of nwords << 2, and the DMA iteration count became nwords instead of that byte count. The S32K1xx LPSPI driver has the same DMA exchange code before that fix: it computes nbytes = nwords << 2 and uses it as the eDMA major loop count for both channels, while each loop moves one 16-bit word. With CONFIG_S32K1XX_LPSPI_DMA enabled and 16-bit words, a transfer above the DMA threshold therefore clocks four times as many words as requested, reads past the end of the transmit buffer and very likely writes past the end of the receive buffer, corrupting memory. The whole imxrt commit (the shift and the two config.iter lines) can be carried over with only the names changed. This is judged from the code only; nothing was built or run on hardware.

 1671  
 1672    if (priv->rxdma == NULL || priv->txdma == NULL

evidence: The imxrt commit 'Fix correct LPSPI DMA transfer size for 16-bit' changes the word-to-byte conversion from nwords << 2 to nwords << 1 ('Fix byte count calculation for 16-bit SPI words using shift-by-1 instead of shift-by-2') and, in the same commit, sets config.iter to nwords for both DMA channels ('Use word count instead of byte count for DMA iteration config'). s32k1xx_lpspi_exchange (the CONFIG_S32K1XX_LPSPI_DMA variant) has exactly the pre-fix code: nbytes = (priv->nbits > 8) ? nwords << 2 : nwords, used for the DMA threshold and as config.iter of both the RX and TX channels, while each minor loop moves config.nbytes = adjust = 2 bytes with 16-bit transfers. The s32k1xx eDMA header documents iter as the major loop iteration count and nbytes as the bytes per minor loop, so for nbits > 8 the DMA runs 4 * nwords 16-bit transfers, four times the 2 * nwords bytes of the caller's buffers. Words wider than 8 bits are valid here (setbits accepts 2..4096 bits and the exchange comment says such data is packed into uint16_t), the DMA path is a normal Kconfig option (S32K1XX_LPSPI_DMA), and nothing else in the function compensates, so the fix applies unchanged apart from names.

title: The Microchip DMAC G2 driver does not copy the new descriptor into the write-back descriptor in dma_mchp_config, so dma_get_status can report a stale pending length after configuration.
summary: On 2026-05-11 the G1 driver (dma_mchp_dmac_g1.c) was fixed to copy the source address, destination address and beat count of the freshly built descriptor into the write-back descriptor in dma_mchp_config and in reload, because dma_get_status reads the remaining length from the write-back descriptor whenever the channel is not the active one. The G2 driver already does this copy in dmac_desc_reload_block, but its dma_mchp_config still stops after dma_mchp_desc_setup without touching descriptors_wb[channel]. As a result, a dma_get_status call on G2 after dma_config, while the channel is not the active one, returns the beat count left in the write-back area by an earlier transfer (zero at boot) instead of the newly configured length, which is the 'stale pending_length' the commit message describes and can mislead callers that compute transferred bytes from pending_length. The fix is to add the same three assignments (plus the typed desc/desc_wb pointers) after dma_mchp_desc_setup in G2's dma_mchp_config; the multi-block check from the same hunk set is already present in G2, so only part of the picked change is needed.

fix.subject: drivers: dma: mchp_dmac_g1: fix callback invocation and status reporting

evidence: The commit message says 'dma_get_status returned stale pending_length after config/reload because write-back descriptor was not synced with base descriptor. Sync write-back in dma_mchp_config and dmac_desc_reload_block.' In dma_mchp_dmac_g2.c, dma_mchp_config (lines 437-469) builds the channel descriptor with dma_mchp_desc_setup(dev_data, config, base_desc) at line 455 and never copies SRCADDR/DSTADDR/BTCNT into descriptors_wb[channel], exactly like g1 before the fix, while dma_mchp_get_status returns data->descriptors_wb[channel].DMAC_BTCNT whenever the channel is not the active one (line 686), the same logic g1 had. G2 uses the same write-back area (DMAC_WRBADDR at line 135) and already syncs it in dmac_desc_reload_block ('Sync WB registers', line 247), so every field and struct the fix needs exists on this side; only the config path lacks it, and the fixed g1 driver still does this sync in its config at the pinned commit (g1 lines 515-518). Of the three picked hunks, the void* to typed-pointer change is cosmetic and the block_count > 1 check of the first hunk already exists in g2 (line 344); the write-back sync of the third hunk (with the declarations from the second) is the part that is missing.

title: The STM32 OSPI flash driver never falls back to the 4 KiB sector size in its page layout when the flash reports no erase type, because BIT(0) is 1, not 0.
summary: On 2026-09-16 (commit 0b92a79e) the STM32 XSPI flash driver fixed setup_pages_layout so that, when no erase type is found, the layout uses SPI_NOR_SECTOR_SIZE instead of a one-byte erase size. The STM32 OSPI driver has the same function with the old code: it computes BIT(value) and only falls back when the result is 0, which never happens. When the flash's SFDP tables leave no erase type, the OSPI page layout reports the 256-byte program page as the erase page, while the driver's erase function refuses any size that is not a multiple of 4 KiB. Code that erases one layout page at a time through the flash page layout would then get an error. The change is a one-line copy with the same names.

fix.subject: drivers: flash: stm32: xspi: fix XSPI page layout fallback

evidence: The XSPI hunk replaces `erase_size = BIT(value)` plus the `if (erase_size == 0)` fallback with `(value != 0U) ? BIT(value) : SPI_NOR_SECTOR_SIZE`; the commit message says "When no erase type is found, the erase exponent remains zero. Applying BIT(0) produces an incorrect one-byte erase size and prevents the fallback to SPI_NOR_SECTOR_SIZE." setup_pages_layout in flash_stm32_ospi.c (line 1785) is the same pre-fix code: value starts at 0, is only taken from erase types whose cmd is non-zero, and BIT(value) is then compared with 0, which can never be true because BIT(n) is (1UL << (n)) in include/zephyr/sys/util_macro.h. The OSPI driver can end up with no usable erase type: it memsets erase_types before decoding the BFP and sets cmd to 0 for every type the 4-byte address instruction table marks 0xff (line 2558); then erase_size is 1, the compatibility check at line 1811 never fires, and the layout keeps data->page_size (default SPI_NOR_PAGE_SIZE, 0x100) as its page size. flash_stm32_ospi_erase meanwhile rejects any size that is not a multiple of SPI_NOR_SECTOR_SIZE (line 1195) and falls back to a 4 KiB sector erase, so the reported page cannot be erased on its own. The fix only uses SPI_NOR_SECTOR_SIZE, which the same OSPI function already uses, and nothing else in the OSPI driver handles the zero-exponent case.

evidence_refs.quote: .page_size = SPI_NOR_PAGE_SIZE, /* by default, to be updated by sfdp */

title: The ADXL367 trigger thread still has the wrong thread entry signature and is cast to k_thread_entry_t, the pattern the 2023 sensor-wide fix removed from ADXL362 and ADXL372.
summary: On 2023-10-30 (commit 191865b5) Zephyr changed the trigger threads of 50 sensor driver files, including ADXL362 and ADXL372, to take (void *p1, void *p2, void *p3) instead of a driver data pointer, and removed the cast to k_thread_entry_t when creating the thread. The ADXL367 driver, written from the same ADI trigger code, still declares adxl367_thread with a struct pointer parameter and casts it at k_thread_create. Starting a thread through a function pointer of another type is undefined in C, but this thread never returns, so the stack corruption on thread exit that the commit describes cannot happen here and behaviour most likely stays the same. The fix can be copied as is with the names changed.

+			adxl362_thread, drv_data,

k_thread_create(&drv_data->thread, drv_data->thread_stack,

evidence: Commit 191865b5 ("Fix thread function signatures to avoid stack corruption on thread exit") changed adxl362_thread and adxl372_thread from taking a struct pointer to the k_thread_entry_t form (void *p1, void *p2, void *p3), and dropped the (k_thread_entry_t) cast at k_thread_create; both source drivers still have that form. adxl367_trigger.c, a sibling of the same ADI trigger code, still has the pre-fix pattern in both places: `static void adxl367_thread(struct adxl367_data *drv_data)` at line 70 and `(k_thread_entry_t)adxl367_thread, drv_data,` at line 178, where k_thread_entry_t is `void (*)(void *p1, void *p2, void *p3)` (include/zephyr/arch/arch_interface.h:46), so the thread is started through a function pointer of a different type. Nothing in the ADXL367 driver handles this another way, and the fix only needs ARG_UNUSED and a local pointer, which are available. The runtime effect is small: the code is only built with the non-default ADXL367_TRIGGER_OWN_THREAD option, and the thread body is `while (true)` and never returns, so the "thread exit" case named in the commit cannot occur here; what remains is a call through a mismatched function type, which C leaves undefined.
impact_note: The thread loops forever and never returns, so the stack corruption on thread exit that the commit names cannot happen here; only the formally undefined call through a mismatched function type remains, and only with the non-default own-thread trigger mode.
